goetrg. HOW THE ROSE CAME. In its green pastures sporting, A lamb in heedless glee, Tore from a thorny twig Its fresh green drapery. ... The twig, in its sharp fingers, Snatched from the tender ewe A little turf of fleece, To clothe itself anew. • A nightingale came seeking' Soft things to line her nest, " And thought this snowy fleece Was prettiest and best.

"0 give to me the fleece, To line my nest," said she; "And when I've finished it, I'll sing my thanks to thee." It gave; the nest wasafinished, And as the sweet bird sang, • Out of the bush for joy The lovely rose-bud sprang. --Froat.the German.
Tarittio.

No man ever arrived suddenly at the summit of vice. If you want to be unhappy, commence fretting about 'he future. I take it that nothing is worth reading that does not require an alert mind. To find the newest books out go to a circulating ibrary. The newest books are always out there. ' The bad traits in character are passed down from generation to generation with as much care as the good 05155. A true friend unbosorns freely, advises justly, assists readily. defends courageously, and continues a friend unchangedly. The surest sign of wisdom is charity: and the best charity is that which never ostensibly parades itself as a charity.—Lord Lytton. A man who can preach wisdom to his neighbour at . the rate of one hundred words a minute, is very often a fool himself, in practice at all events. "I wonder what makes these buttons burst off so?" Dora petulantly exclaimed. David looked at her tight dress. "Force of habit, I think." be said softly. If plants refused to grow in spring, sceptical people would begin to-mend their faith, and yet the regularities of nature are the finger-posts which point to Heaven. When an acquaintance came up to him and said, • Why, Jerrold, I hear you said my nose was like the ace of clubs!" Jerrold returned. "No, I didn't; but, now I look at it, I see it is very file." If a man really loves study and has an eager desire for the acquisition of knowledge, nothing but misfortune or somethieg exceptional in the way of accident will prevent him from being a successful strident. A HEAVENLY FAMILY.—A little four-year-old was much Impressed with her first out-of-doors in the starlight. On her arrival home, she skipped joyfully up to her mother with the glad tidings, "Oh, mama, I've seen the moon and all her little children !", A little girl sat gazing fixedly at the new bonnet of one of her mother's-visitors, until the caller smilingly asked, "Doyen like it, my dear?" The child innocently replied, "Yes, I do. Mamma and Aunt Milly said it was a perfect fright, but it doesn't frighten me a bit." A popular author was sometime back in a bookseller's shop. A smartly-dre.sed lady entered, and inquired for his book. On asking the price, she demurred, remarking "The fact is, I am to meet the author at dinner to-night, and I want to read him up a bit; but he is not worth thirty shillings." A story -urrent regarding the pride of a well-known inzresarto. At a certain rehearsal the tenor said to his chief, "That aria is a little too high for me." "Oh, transpose it a tone!" was the reply. "A half-tone," pursued the tenor, " will suit me perfectly." "Sir," re- torted the manager, proudly drawing himself up; "in my theatre we do nothing by halves," Little Isaac Moses, whose grandfather began life as an errand boy, and finished as a millionaire, was paid by his mother a penny a dozen for rains picked up from the carpet, to keep the baby from getting them. "Nurse," said little Isaac, as his stock of pennies increased, "do you know what lam going to do when I have sixpence?" "No," answered nurse. lam going to buy a paper of pins, and scatter them all over the floor, and then pick them up," replied the young financier, who was barely six years old. Thor conscience can be dulled in one direction by neglect, even while it is quickened in another by exercise; and it is too often the case that persons think themselves bound to pursue a certain course while they entirely forget they are first of all bound to discover, to the beet of their ability, whether that course is the right and true one. To cultivate the reason, to strengthen the judg- ment, to probe conclusions, to examine opinions, are obligations which a sensitive conscience should press with as much urgency as to act up to those conclusions when intelligently formed. A venerable archdeacon was one day in the Colonial Exhibition, and thinking he recognised the back of a friend in the crowd, picked his pocket of a handker- chief by way of a joke. Promptly was the clergyman seized upon by a detective. "Nonsense, my dear man," said the reverend joker, "that's a friend of mine." But when the owner of the handkerchief turned round, he revealed the face of an utter stranger. In vain did the archdeacon protest at the station, and declare his exalted rank. "That won't wash. We've had a Bishop or two 'ere before now," was all the satisfaction he got: and things looked undeniably serious until the arrival of those who could vouch for the identity of the reverend gentleman. A BOY'S LETTER To yrre EMPEROR WILLTAM.—A thirteen-year-old lad, of Stahm, in Prussia, wrote the following letter to the Emperor William on his Majesty's birthday, and it is stated that what the little petitioner asks is likely to be granted:—" Dear King,—On thy great birthday thy subject offers most obedient congra- tulations, with the prayer to the good God that thou mayest long be our good King. And now I beg you be so kind as to send my poor father—who has been an invalid since the war with Austria, having been shot in the foot—something from the war fund. I have two brothers and two sisters, and often we have no bread to eat. I, like my brother, mean to be a soldier, and then will fight the enemy. My dear mother has long been sick. And now I greet you. dear Emperor, and send you my name.—AcaysT WOLK, thirteen years old." A LEAP-YEAR EPISODE—They were seated in the par- lour, and the clock had struck the hour of ten. They were an economical young couple, never utilising but one chair for both to sit upon, and he always clasped his arms about her waist to prevent her from falling off. The young lady was handsome, and she was exceedingly clever, as the sequel will show; while her male com- panion was as stupid as a goose. She was rather tall and slender, had bright blue eyes, rosy cheeks, blonde hair, and invariably wore a mauve-coloured silk dress. They had discussed the weather probabilities, her papa's rheumatic paralysis, her dear mamma's neuralgia, and all the other stereotyped topics, interspersed now and then with a long-drawn sigh or a kiss, and the conversa- tion began to drag wearily on. At last a bright idea entered her little head, whereby she could infuse interest into the evening's entertainment, and, besides, bring a very important point before the court. She said; "Did you ever study palmistry ?" " Well, Nellie, I've studied mostly all of ihesclassics, ' he replied, "but I can't !lay that I devoted any time to that branch. Of what does it treat ?' "Why," murmured Nellie, "it is an art whereby you can tell a person's future by examining the palm of the hand. Would you like to know your future?" • I haven't the slightest objection." She took his hand gently in hers, and, after making v careful diagnosis of the creases in it, said "You come of a long-liven family; your grandfather lived to be 82- years of age, and your grandmother 75; your father and mother are still living —" "Why, Nellie," interrupted George, "I told you all of that the other night." "Well, that does not make the slightest bit of difference. I could inform you of the fact by this art, supposing you had never told me any- thing about it. But pardon the digression. You will probably live to be 71 years of age or thereabouts; you are desperately in love with a sweet young girl, but too bashful to pop the momentous question; there are two or three suitors for her hand, but she is yours, and yours only (sighing) ; she loves you, dear George. with that xri idd suing flame which can only be the luscious fruit of a trusting young heart; she would make you a good wife (pressing his hand softly) ; in sickness she would be ever found at your bedside caring for you, and you could not do better than marry her; she is tall and slender, has bright blue eyes, rosy cheeks, blonde hair, dresses in mauve-coloured silk—" "Stop!" shrieked George, "I can stand it no longer. Will you be mine?" And she be-mined. BY H. Warms:lG (Concluded) In my last I made reference to the evidence of Mr. Alfred Hewlett, given before the Royal Commission, wherein be stated that "Royalties in England are feur times as high as in Westphalia." Rather than interfere with the owners of the English royalties this gentleman. managing director of the Wigan Coal and Iron Company, could only give as an opinion that "for the collier I think the rate of wages ought to be reduced." Since this very wise opinion was given, a largely attended meeting of the West Lan. eaahire Coal Owners Association, has been held at the North Western Hotel, Liverpool, Mr. A. Hewlett in the chair, at which it was resolied that. a reduction in the wages of the colliers was absolutely necessary, and a committee of the masters was appointed to meet the reen's representatives on the subject. So the game goes on. To him that bath shall be given, but to him that bath not, the little that he has shall be taken away. In a very able art cle in the " Manchester Guardian" on the currency question the writer states: We are far from desiring to See a further decline in wages, but apart from a'revival of trade and a check to the downward course of prices we do not see what forces there are which cin be relied upon to prevent a continued fall in the value of labour." Mr. Giffen warns us that "a further decline In the value of labour must be t xpected." It remains for workmen to ask can this process go on indefinitely? There are those who say that "labour will gain nothing by trusting to politics." Politics is the science of life. .Through politics may come peaceful and bloodless revolutions. A politician to day should have a pretty fair grasp of all questions relating to the commonweal, and a can- didate for .parlianientary honour + should in no case be accepted who has not made it his duty to study the labour question. To represent a brewery, to sit in the House twenty years without once addressing his -constituency on questions relating to their every day life, should be sufficient to entitle a roan to instant dismiseal. To refuse, as Sir Gilbert Greenal did, to meet a deputation on the question of royalties -argued one of two things. He either knew nothing of the subject, or he prefers matters to remain as they are. If the former, he is not capable of representing this borough; and if the latter, well—whatever comes to is as workingmen will serve us right if we allow him , to remain where he is _ _ _

It is a remarkable feature that each member of Parlia- ment at all familiar with the land question, and its incl. dents is Radical, and all are members of one or other of the many land reform associations that have been recently formed. Let us see what a few of them say on the general question of royalties. Mr. Stephen Mason, who represents, one of the Lanarkshire division, states the case of a ducal leesh who extracts no less than £ll4-000 per aneum from the mining industry. This duke grants leases for twenty- one yews at fixed "rents" varying from £5OO to £5,000. These must be paid whether the mine is worked or not. If worked, the moment a certain output is attained "royalties" commence. These vary from 9d to 1s 6.1 per ton. Again, he says one company spent £50,000 to get at a seam of coal. They reached it, but found that rent and royalty would together absorb every penny of profit. The landlord insieted on his pound of flesh ; the consequence was that the I machinery was stopped, and has stood idle far four years.. Mr. Conyheare, a Cornwall representative, gives similar instances, one of which, for the renewal of a lease (the Dol- math mine), £25,000 was exacted. Again, the Duke of Bed- ford, In the CaSB of the Devon Great Consels Mine, levied a fine of £20,000. I wish my fellow workmen to take part'. eller notice of these figures, and to put two and two to- gether, and see how the result affects their wages. In the last named case, if the lessees had refused to be black- mailed by this most noble duke he would have taken their enema houses and all the company's improvements without giving any compensation whatever. It is almost impossible to get at t!-.e exict figures as to what is the nation'e tribute to the land har- pies for the right to WuT k the nation's na- tural Storer, but it is eetimated that in 1883, they pocketed on coal and iron ore alone the enormous sum of eight miltions sterling. Think of it, working-men, eight millions in ens year. In Scotland the minimum royalty is 61 per ton on pig iron, and in Cleveland 38 3d. The consequence is Cleveland sends weekly to Scotland from 6,000 to 7,000 tons. In a recent address by Mr. Furavtb, president of the Scottish Land Restoration League, he said, "They might be idle for want ef capital; they might be idle for want of men willing to work. Well, gen- tlemen, the Cumberland furnaces are put out not becauee of any lack of capital, for only within the last week or two a company of employers there were willing to siek £200,000 in raising ore, and were only prevented from doing so by the landlord's ultimatum that he would not reduce his royalty of 2s 6d per ton on the ore which might be raised. The company could not pay this charge, and imported ore more cheaply from Spain." Girders and tram rails are imported and laid ie all our large towns. One ironmaeter, the owner of eight furnaces specially adapted for the manufacture of pig-iron and steel rails, keeps four of these furnaces idle, and imports thou- sands of tons of iron and steel from Belgium and Germany. I am anxious to draw these facts poietedly before the atten- tion at my fellow workmen, as I hold they have a remedy in their hands for slack times and low wages. The English workmen, with their employers' commercial knowledge, are capable of ruling the whole trading world if they will pnly use it. Suppose a blast furnace to produce six hundred tons of pig iron a week, the landlord's royalty would amount to £202, and the wages of five different classes of workmen would amount to only £.95. The royalty paid on British steel rails amounts to 93 61 per ton; in Belgium the average is Is 9d, and yet the Indian De- partment is yearly sending out to India thou- sands of tons of imported iron and steel rails and sleepers. It is stated that "a Cunard liner making the double or return journey across the Atlantic consumes four thousand one hundred and twenty-five toes of coal. This means a royalty to the landlord of £206 se, or more than the wages of the entire crew from captain to cabin boy." The owners of steamers pay to those who toil not, neither do they spin, the !elm of £2,751,000 per annum ; most people would call this blackmail. Mr. Conybeare's sliding scale between land- lords and mine lessees will never cure this, unless the State is the landlord. In Scotland there is an Act dating from 1592, which the landlords put aside, which gives the power to appoint a Master of the metals" with full state con- trol of all mines and minerals in the realm, and which ex- empts miners from all taxation whatever, both in peace and war, and gives the Sovereign Lord power to take into his care their families and goods in case of accidents. Summarised the facts are these ; with regard to iron, in I the last five or six years, the royalty paid upon the ore, Icoal, limestone, fire clay, tic., used, brings up the royalty to upon a ton of hematite iron on the west coast to 63 61 a ton, the royalty on a ton of ore being about 28 61. The iron used on the east coast is not taxed to the same extent, the ore nsed there being from Bilbao in Spain, where the royalty is only 8d a ton, thus giving (for two tons of ore to one of pig-iron) a royalty, so far as ore is concerned, of Is ld a ton only, as compared with 5s Id which is paid at Barrow on the west coast. 'The royalties of, Barrow have increased of late years in spite of the decrease in the price of iron. In high-price times royalties as high as fle or lOs a ton were charged its the Cumberland district. In Lancashire, the royalty starts at 23. for a 123. value, but is reduced if the price sinks lower, 80 that at Bs. value it is is a ton ; but if the price rises ahove 12e. the royalty rises very rapidly. As things stand at present, all that would be profit, and go towards making a wage for the workman, goes into the landlord's pocket. At the Trades Union Congress, held at Hull last year, it was stated that the 'landlords received a royalty of 6d, per tin coal, and the mines' inspectors' report lately showed there had been raised 159,000,000 tons in the year 1885. Putting the years 1884 and 1885 together, it .would be seen that 320,000 000 tone had been railed, and that there was an average of 520,504 men and boys working in the mines. If they put these tons into money they bad £2,677,576 going into the landlords pockets in two years, and dividing that Bum it would yield a sum of £5 28 Bd to every man, woman, and boy employed about the pits." The prices paid to colliers per ton varies considerably, eeldom reacning chiefly ranging from 6d to Bd, so that the landlerd pockets as much from underground rents as the poor collier, of whose sad end we so often hear throu.tia accidents and ex• plosion&

OUlt LONDON LETTER.
LONDON THURSDAY.

Readers of this column will know that from the earliest and most important attempt at re-union of the Liberal party, that in which the Round Table figured, I have taken a pessimistic view of the situ- ation:. Having some personal acquaintance with the personages concerned, I have been reluctantly driven to the conclusion that as long as Mr. Glad- stone lives there will be no re-union with his old colleakues. Mr. Gladetone has the gift of inspiring .strong personal attachment or equally strong per- sonal antipathy. I am .bound to say that the former operates chiefly on the vest and more distant edges of his acquaintance; whilst the antipathy is mani- fested in the inner circle of those who come in actual contact with him. He has not the gift Mr. Disraeli possessed of personally attaching people to him. Why this is so is a matter too intricate and delicate to be discussed here. But the fact remains. Whilst, as was recently shown in his tour through Wales, Mr: Gladstone s presence exercises a mag- netic influence on the multitude; he is not as popu- lar in the House of Commons, though his genius constantly demands its applause. By a very large Timber of people he is intensely hated, and in that number is now included his old colleagues, •Lard Hartington, Mr. Chamberlain, and, as a recent un- necessarily acrimonious letter shows, Mr. Bright. • Mr. Gladstone has made up his mind, with the help of the country, to return to power. Lord Bar- tington, Mr. Chanberlain, Mr. Bright and a score of others, formerly holding more or less prominent positions in his following, have determined that he shall not. Inoredible as it may appear. the ques- tion is a personal one raging round the individu- ality of the great Liberal leader. If Mr. Gladstone's Career were closed to-morrow, I believe the \Har- tington-Chamberlain-Bright alliance with the Tories would melt away in a week, and before the session closed the Government would be defeated. But Mr. Gladstone does not mean to disappear vet. He is in excellent health and spirits, and takes great care nf himself. What he looks forward to is a general. election, and firmly believes that between him and his revolted lieutenants the people will by acclama- tion declare in his favour. The Dissentient Liberals, on their part, fear a general election, at which they can be saved only by the good offices of the Tories. This apprehension operates.to the advantage of the Government, who, if they can keep Mr. Chamber- lain and Mr. Bright in tow are in for aplonged term of office. ,

An English member of the House of Commons who has just been over to Ireland to investigate matters for himself takes a very gloomy view of the prospects. He tells me that he found widely spread,indisputable, evidence of a resolve to pro- ceed to the utmost limits of the law against ten- ants who cannot or will not pay their rents. It is not so much on the part of landlords that this de- termination exists as that of the land agents. In many cases the landlord is in the power of the land agent, who has made money advances and taken the rents in pawn. It is the agent's own money that is at stake, and with the assistance of the Coercion Bill they mean to get it. The pro- ceedings at Bodyke are shocking enough: but ac- cording to ray informant they are only the precur- sor of scenes that will, as the year advances, deso- late Ireland. The tenants have had their Plan of ' Campaign, and now the agents and the landlords have formulated theirs. The Coercion Bill will make the opposition of the landlords finally irre- sistable ; but before victory is achieved there will be things done in Ireland that may have important results through the operation of excited public feeling in Great Britain. The ultimate conclusion of the whole matter is inevitable. Ireland will get Home Rule, but in the meantime the Dissentient Liberals have placed a Conservative -Government in a position to recur to its traditional policy in Ire- land, and there will be sad times both for Ireland and England to go through before the goal is reached.

London along the route of the Jubilee procession presents just now an extraordinary sight. It is handed over to the carpenters and the gas men. The amount of timber used for setting up grand stands is prodigious. Every private house on the route has its little gallery set forth before the first floor window, and every club and shop and place of business its grand; stand. The prices asked for favoureu positions are, , one would think, prohibi- tive. But there is as •y‘t no sign of falling away. The somewhat tardY debision of the Government to erect a grand stand in St. Stephen's-square should have had the effect of weakening prices. But there is no evidence as yet that it has done so. Those who cannot obtain seats in Westminster Abbey are wisely, and not without reason, convincing them- selves that, after all, the thing to see is the proces- sion wending its way through the crowded streets, and, not least, the multitude who will come out to

see the show. Of course the measure of the success will depend upon the fineness of the weather. But there is another contingency upon which little is. said, though a great deal is thought by those per- sonally concerned in the pageant. Latest news from Berlin represents the Emperor of Germany as in better health: But a few days ago his condition was very critical. People are asking what would ' happen to the Jubilee show if the aged Emperor were to die on its eye? It is pretty certain that, if the Queen did not decide to postpone the ceremony, it would in such case be shorn of mueh of its pic- torial air. There was, by the way, one touch of real humour in Mr. Cbamberlain's speech on Tuesday. He more than once alluded to the great body of the Liberal party from which he has cut himself adrift as "the Gladstonian Dissentients." This reminds me of a story told at Earl's Court about Red Shirt. In his earlier days this famous Indian was discovered by a party of scouts wandering in the depth of the forest hungry and tired. "Are you lost ? " asked the scouts. "No," said the imperturbable Indian, "Me no lost. Me here; wigwam lost." Thus it is with Mr. Chamberlain and his scanty muster of friends. They are not Dissentients. It is the great body from which they have separated themselves that are Dissentients. ' _ The Jubilee Ball at the Reform Club. which lasted

far ln-tO this morning was -------------------- TO; 271 M-3-7 things, its not least striking peculiarity being that it was a ball at. which there was no dancing. There was a hand and a capital floor and many hundreds of couples who did, now and then, periodically at- tempt a waltz. But the surging crowd was so overwhelming, that there was scarcelyroom to turn round. I fancy, however, that only a very incon- siderable portion of the brilliant throng really went to dance. It is not often in contemporary history that such a gathering of notable personages is en- closed within the four walls of a building, and there was quite enough pleasant occupation in strolling round and gazing akthe moving scene. The place itself was so tranaforined that old habitues were found wandering about in a lost condition. The great surprise was the terrace garden, beautifully illuminated, presenting a fairy scene as the gaily- dressed ladies strolled about and jewels flashed like fireflys in the sultry air. Here the Prince of Wales sat for a long time chatting to his son, Prince Albert Victor, the Duke of Cambridge, Earl Granville, and others. Next to the garden the surprise was to see so many Conservatives. Lady Salisbury had a reception at the Foreign Office, and thence towards midnight came a stream of the principal personages, including Mr. W. H. Smith, the Lord Chancellor, the Solicitor-General, Sir Henry Holland, Baron de Worms, and scores of the rank and file Of the great Conservative party. Nor were the Dissentient Liberals lacking. Mr. Chamberlain, of course, will have nothing to do with the Reform Club, which once declined the . _ _

div.head: STATEMENTS BY THE UNDER-SCRETARY.
div.p: STATEMENTS BY THE UNDER-SCRETARY.

Mr. Dittow said that the Irish members were prepared to prove, by the testimony of independent English eye- witnesses, that the replies given to questions in that House, and the statements there made by the Under- Secretary to the Lord-Lieutenant, in regard to the occurrence at Bodyke, were absolutely false. He wanted to know whether the Chief-Secretary would inform the House of the source of his information, and place before the House the telegrams he had received on the subject. Mr. A. J. Iletvoun declined to produce the telegrams which had passed between the Irish Office in Dublin and the Irish Office in London in regard to the Bodyke evic- tions. He did not know how the hon. member proposed to prove that the statements made by the Under-Secre- tary were false. If he proposed to ask for a day to do this in that House then his request should be addressed to the Leader of the House. The best course would be for the hon. member to furnish the Government with the proofs that he possessed of the inaccuracy of the Under- Secretary's statements, and the Government would then consider what should be done.
Mr. DILLON said that he should not be satisfied with this, but that he and his friends would consider how the matter could be brought before the Hoe,..e THE CRIMES BILL.
Committee on the Criminal Law Amendment (Ireland) 11111 was resumed at Clause 6.
A number of aMendments.were moved and rejected

Dr. Commes moved to omit the words which enabled the Lord-Lieutenant to proclaim any association inter- fering with the administration of the law, or disturbing the maintenance of law and order. This part of the clause contained, he contended, a whole Coercion Act in itself.—Sir W. HARCOURT wanted to know what, if this clause were passed without amendment, was to be anticipated of the action of the Government against such a society as the Anti-Vaccination Society. Would that he asked, be regarded as one for resisting the law? He condemned the vagueness of the phraseology employed by the Government'in the construction of the clause, and pointed out that the Lard Chancellor, who was the adviser of the Lord-Lieutenant, had been de- clared to be wrong in a decision The had given by four of the Irish judge,s. Mr. A. J. 13,ktrourt expressed the utmost surprise that a late Home Secretary should have waited till 11 20 to discuss principles that had been under dismission all the evening. (Ministerial cheers.) The Lord Chancellor never had been the chief adviser of the Government on the Irish policy. (Ministerial cheers and derisive cheers from the Opposition.) The ground on which the right hon. gentleman had based his attack deserved severe censure. The Lord Lieutenant could do nothing under the clause being discussed, in which he would not have the sanction of the representatives of the majority of the British people. (Cheers and derisive cheers.) Mr. J. MORLEY expressed the utmost surprise at the language of the Chief Secretary, whose view of the posi- tion of the Lord Chancellor of Ireland in regard to the Executive Government was amazing. When the Lord- Lieutenant was absent from Ireland, the chief es- officio officer was .the Lord Chancellor. (Hear, hear.) According to the Chief Secretary, they were not to con- sider the effect of this or any other part of the bill as a portion of a great legal instrument, but rather whether it was approved by a fleeting and temporary majority of the House. (Opposition cheers.) This was the true Tory doctrine—(loud Opposition cheers)—bitt, a doctrine the Opposition would do all they could to pro Vest against. (Cheers.) After some remarks from Dr. Comtnins and Mr. Molloy, Sir W. Hammerer denounced as absolutely without prece- dent the language the Committee had just heard from the Treasury bench, in which the doctrine had been pro- claimed that a criminal statute might be passed giving to the Executive Government any sort of powers, how- ever vague and undefined, and that those powers would I be safe if only sanmioned by a majority of the House. ! The amendment was negatived by ne to 140. Mr. Fm-LAY proposed to leave out 'in this Act referred to as a dangerous association." As -he read the 6th and 7th clause there was no limit to the power of the Lord Lieutenant, and he might put down any association. The amendment he proposed required that the Lord Lieutenant should specify the association to be sul-)- pressed. Mr. A. Batrotrn said the Government would accept the first of the series of amendments proposed by the hon. member, but it must not be assumed that they would agree to all the consequential amendments. Mr. Locawoon protested against the solemn farce the Committee had just witnessed. (Radical cheers.) It was clear the amendment was agreed to before it was proposed. The amendment was then agreed to without a division. . _ . .

During the discussion or an amendment by Mr. Clancy,. Mr. W. H. Surru moved to report progress. Mr. CHANCE said that under the rule passed on Satur- day morning no motion to report progress could he made except by a Minister whose name appeared on the bill. (Laughter and Parnellite cheers.) The right hon. gentle- man's name did not appear on the bill. Mr. A. Ratrorm then made the motion for progress, and it was agreed to. CROFTERS' HOLDINGS. The Crofters' Holdings (Scotland) Bill NM read a second time.
The Rouse adjourned at 2 10 a.m. HOUSE OP COMMONS.—WEDNESDAY. The Speaker took the chair at 12 o'clock. THE COERCION BILL.

Mr. APNErt. resumed the discussion on Mr. Chance's amendment to the sixth clause of the Criminal Law (Ire- land) Amendment Bill, and criticised the constitution of the Privy Council in Dublin. Several Irish members continued the debate.—Sir W. HARCOuni did not think the point was worth discussing at any great length. it was the nee to say that certain acts were done by order of the Queen in Council and were promulgated with the assent of the Crown, but the real responsibility rested on the Minister. It was the same in Ireland, and he did not think the point was worth considering.—The ATTORNEY-GENERAL for IRELAND contended that the action of the Privy Coun- cil in Ireland was precisely the same as in England.—Even- tually the amendment was withdrawn—Mr. FINLAY moved an amendment, the effect of which was that the association or associations proclaimed should be specially named in the proclamation.—Mr. BALFOUR opposed the amendment, and after considerable discussion the House divided, when there voted for the amendment 145, ag iinst it 190.—Mr. CHANCE moved an amendment providing that a special proclama- tion shall define the district, or districts, to which it ap- plies.—The ATTORNEY-GENERAL for IRELAND could not accept the amendment.-Dr. Commies and Mr M Healey fol- limed, and the House divided, with the result that the amendment was rejected, 152 members voting for it and 217 against—Amendments moved by Mr. M. Healey and Dr. Commies were also negatived, and the House adjourned at six o'clock.

_ HOUSE OF LORDS —THURSDAY. The Lord Chancellor took his seat on the woolsack at quarter after four o'clock. COTTAGERS ALLOTMENTS.—In the House of Lords last night the Earl of DIINRAVEN, in moving the second reading of the Allotments for Cottagers Bill, said he did not wish to create small holdings but allotments, or rather small plots which the agricultural labourer could cultivate and on which he could use his spare time without interfering in any way with his capacity as a wage-earner, and as merely supplementary to his ordinary employment. The bill provided that the allotments should not exceed one and that they should be situated as near as possible to the cottages of the labour- ers, that they should be let at reasonable and fair rents, that the demand for them should be bona-fide one, and that if it was necessary to take up land compulsorily no injustice or pecuniary 1088 should be en- tailed on the owners of land. It was further explained that the bill would not allow an unfair quantity of land to he taken from one landowner, and that land which for special reasons was exceptionally valuable would not be affected'. ' The duty of administering the measure it was proposed to entrust for the present to the magistrates in Quarter See- -1 sions, to be transferred to the county boards when they are established. Whatever advances were made would he on the security of the county rates:—The Marquis of SALISBURY, though he was anxious to see the problem dealt with in the Bill pushed on in a legitimate way, said he did not intend now to state what the Government Bill would be. He , thought one acre was too large for a single allotment. With regard to the adthority to whom the administration of a bill of this kind should be entrusted, he should prefer to I adopt the local authority which would be provided in the propoNd County Government Bill. Though he was willing to give the bill a second reading, he must not be taken as assenting to its details. The bill was then read a second time. Their Lordships adjourned at fifteen minutes past six o'clock. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—TanuspeT.

-- - The Speaker took the chair at 4-0. Quvsnotqs, &c.—Colonel KING-FURMAN informed Mr. Dillon, in reply to a question, that the liovernment were not aware of any circumstances connected with the recent proceedings at Bodyke to justify the appointment of a Select Committee.—Mk STANHOPE promised to lay on the table such a memorandum, explaining the charges made by Lord R. Churchill against the Ordnance Department, as would place the House in possession of the fullest information on the points raised. Mr. SMITH said he should feel it his duty, as soon as the state of pub- lic business permitted, to afford the House an opportunity of discussing the . memorandum. The right hon. gentleman, replying to Colonel Stndys, stated that in a letter addressed by Cardinal Howard to the Secre- tary for Foreign Affairs, the Pope intimated his intention of sending a mission to congratulate her Majesty on the occa- sien of her Jubilee, and Lord Salisbury had replied that it would give her Majesty pleasure to receive the envoy. He

would be received on the same footing as missions from the Pope were received at rtther Courts in Europe, txdh Plotest- ant and Catholic, and no law was required to enable her P.l,jesty to receive such a mission. Mr. Smith informed the House that the Government had decided that the Criminal Law Amendment (Ireland) Bill should not be taken next week.

IIODYKE EVICTIONS.—Upon Mr. Dtrzotr proposing, as a matter ot public urgency, to call attention to the recent evictions at Bodyke and the conduct of the police in carry- ing them out, a number of the Tory members walked out of the HOuse. The hon. member for Mayo proceeded to state that the evictions on Colonel O'Callaghan's estate had been carried out in a most brutal manner, and he defined the Government to find a single Englishman who had investiga- ted the circumstances of the case who would drclate that right was not en the side of the tenants.—Mr. BALFOUR ObjeClSl to the action of ben. members in forcing on this discussion when they knew that the Government was not yet in possession of full materials for a reply. As to these evictions, if Colonel O'Callaghan had asked his advice they would probably never have taken place. He declared that these evictions had been used for tie purposes of political agitation, and protested against the doctrine that the remedy for a law which In some cases was harshly exercised was that that law should be broken. —Mr. Viremil gave examples from personal ob- servation of wrongs inflicted upon tenants on Colonel O'Callaghan's estate He called upon the Government not merely to try to stifle the cry of the victims, but to re- move the wrong they were suffering under.—Mr. MORLEY said he was very much mistaken if the facts which had been elated would not have a very important effect upon the judgment which the constituencies would pronounce upon the policy of the Government.—The BONE b'EClte- TART admitted that, presuming the facts stated were true, some of the cases were intolerably hard, and sad he be lleved the case of the Bodyke estate was entirely excep- tional —The House was afterwards addressed by Lord B. Churchill, Mr. John Morley, Mr. S. W. Lawson, and others, and on a division the numbers were—For Mr. Dillon's mo- tion, 165; against, 246. THE CRIMES Bict.—Upon the order for the Coercion Bill being called by the Clerk at the Table, Mr. W. H. Sigma moved that it be postponed till to-morrow (Friday). The House adjourned at half-past one,

TUG OF WAR —Six employes of Messrs N Matthieson & Co. (captain, J Brooks) beat six employes of the Widnes Alkali Company, Limited (captain, W Harrison), and were in turn defeated by another six employes of the Alkali Company (ciptain, Peter Dawson), who won the first prize. The first prizes were six cases of spoons and tongs, and the second prizes six teapots. FOOTBALL CONTEST.—The first match was Runcorn v. Widnes, The latter team was composed as on the previous evening, when they defeated Farnworth. Runcorn team was as follows :—Brazendale, fall back; H Speakman, T Davies, three-qaarters ; H Andrews, half back; Broady, Wainwright, Faulkner, and Abrams, forwards. The game was a very fast one, and although Runcorn had the advan- tage. Widnes drew first blood by scoring a dead ball. Davies retaliated by making a splendid run to Widnes lines, where he was collared. From scrimmage, Andrews got hold, and got over the Bee. Speakman brought out the ball, and Widoes objected to a kick at goal being allowed because Speakman had not made his mark. The referee upheld the objection. The place was beautifully situated for ecoring a goal, and this mistake undoubtedly lost the Cheshire tam the game, as Widnes added another touch down, made the game drawn by a try (four points) to two minors. During the extra ten minutes that was played, Widnes overshadowed their opponents, and Smith, Plump- ten, and Farrell each scored a try. Final result : Widnes 1 goal, 2 tries. and 2 minors, to 1 try. Warrington baying a walk over with tatherland, opposed the Chemicals after an interval. The Wevringron team was made up as fol- lows:—Nevins, full back ; Massey and blley, three-quarters; Antrobus, half back; Davies, Cralgen, Unsworth, amd Littlewond, forwards. The game was very closely con- tested, and the excitement amongst the spectators was most intense. When time was called, Widnes were in a mejority of two minors to nil. An extra ten minutes to be played, and whilst Widnes succeeded in adding two other minors. Warrington only managed to score 1, and were thus de- feated by 4 minors to 1. At the conclusion of the sports, the prizes were presented to the eucceesful competitors by Mrs. C. E. Barlow, who was previously presented, on behalf of the Athletic Club, with a beautiful bouquet of flowers by Captain Wareing.

gILVER ON THE BRAlN.—Senater Fair, one of the L--7 richest men in the &snails of the United States, being worth over one hundred millions of dollars, lea man of marked pem- liarities. He is largely interested in silver mining, and in more senses than one may be said to have 'silver on the brain," for about the commencement of his successful career, he received a blow which frac ured his skull, and was only saved from death by the operation of trepanning—that is to say, a plate of silver was inserted in the top of his head. Tie is still a young man, and though his halr is not "silvered" his skull is; thus differing from many men and women, who have no silver on their brain, but a large supply of it in their hair. People turn grey much ea, lier in life than formerly. Such being the Core. it is surprhing that they do not take better care of it. The hair is a vegetable, and may be cultivated, its growth strength- ened, and:its texture improved by care, attention, and the application of the proper fertilizing -properties. That this is the cm, has been amply demonstrated, and therefore no one , need have thin or grey hair, or a coarse and wiry stubble, provided they will use the proper care. Toe preparation most In vogue fsr this purpose, is und-nbtedly Mrs B. A. APPROACHING MARRIAGE.—A marriage is arranged, and will take place at Eleswall on the 13th July, between Mr. Thomas Woodsend, of Valparaiso, Chili, and Miss ITabella Jane Duncan, only daughter of the late Mr. David Duncan, M.P. In consequence of the recent death of Mr. Duncan, the wedding will be quite quiet, and no invitations will be issued.

THREE CHILDREN CUT TO PIECES.— Three children, named Robert Rees, 13, Morgan Evans, 13, and James Evans, were run over and killed by the 9 35 p.m. pas- senger train on Saturday night, at a point near Victoria Station, Abereorn, on theCrreat Western Railway, their bodies being terribly mutilated. It would appear that the children waited for the 'passing of an up train, but did not observe the approach of the down train.

OPENING OF THE TAY BRIDGE.--:-The Tar Bridge was opened for goods traffic at one o'clock on Monday morn- ing by the passage of a train consisting of a heavy en- gine and forty waggons, which stretched the length of the eleven high girders. During the day trains left for Liverpool, Manchester, and London, and the "deed moat" Loudon express left at ten o'clock on Monday night. Twenty-four trains will pass along ths structure every day this week. A SCHOONER SUNK IN VIE Mknsrx.—Early on Satur- day morning, a serious collision occurred on the Mersey, resulting in the sinking of the schooner Alexander William, which had on board a cargo of coal, and was about to sail to Belfast- Whilst lying at anchor at a point opposite F.gremont, she was run into by the steamship Caxton, from the Elver Plate, and the force of the collision was so great that she soon afterwards sank, having drifted on to the beach at Egremont , Tin DEPUTY POET LATJHEATE.—Owing to the indis- position of Lord Tennyson, the task of writing the inaugural ode on the foundation of the Imperial Institute has been entrusted, through the Prince of Wales, to Mr. Lewis Morris. The ode will be set to music by Sir Arthur Sullivan, and performed on the 4th of July by a 'monster orchestra and chorus at the Albert flaß, in the presence of her Majesty the Queen. Mr. Lewis Morris took a first-c Lass in classics at Oxford in 1845, was called. to the bar in 1:41, and practised chiefly as aconyey- ancingcoamsel until 1880. In 18'79 he became hon. sec- retary et the University College of Wales, and in the following year was appointed on the departmental corn- mittee charged by the Government to inquire into inter- mediate and higher education in the Principality. Be is, however, best known as the author of "Songs of Two .Worlds," "Gwin, a Drama in Monologue," and " The Ode a Life," works which have passed through many edi- tions, and established the reputation of thearauthor.

div.head: WIDNE.'s ATHLETIC CLUB SPORTS.
div.p: WIDNE.'s ATHLETIC CLUB SPORTS.

On Fiirlay evening, the so'h annual festival in con- nection with Widnes Athletic Club, was commenced on the show field, at Faraworth. The weather was extremely favourable for outdoor sports, and at least 1,500 persons assembled as spectators. The various events were confined to competitors who reside within the district, which however comprises the towns with- in a radius of six or seven miles. The arrangements were as complete as in former years, and there were numerous officials present to carry them out. •Mr. T Wilkinson, of Sheffield, was the starter; and Mr. Walter Platt, was the handicapper, official timekeeper, and referee. The duties of judges were performed by Messrs T M Abraham Crews; 0 D Barlow, Widnes; H C Bell, Liverpool; G W Duxfield, Southport ; and Capt. Wareing, Widnes. Particulars of the various events are annexed.

120 YARDS FLAT RACE: let prize, electro plated tea ser- vice, value £5 Se; 2nd electro pitted preserve dish value £2 2e; 3rd, electro plated tankard, value £1 Is. lst heat, 1, W J9ns, Runcorn FO.; 2, Walter Hughes, Garston ; 2nd heat, G T Lever, of St. Helens and J Hartland, Widnes F.C., ran a dead heat. Both competed in the final. 3,d beat: 1, T K Allen, Warrington ; 2, J McLaughlin, St. Helena F.C. Final: 1, T H Allen, (7 yards), 2, W Jones, (7 yards). 3, J Hartland, (8 yards). FOOTBALL COMPETITIONS. The Football contests, 8 aside, proved a most interesting item in the programme. The first corrp«tition was between Widnes F.C. and Farnworth F.C. The Widnes team was composed as follows: full back, Bingham ; three-quarter, Plumpton and Parkinson; half- back, Farrell; forwards Kiddie, (captain,) Hughes, Smith, and Hardman. Faroworth, full ball, W Burgess; three- quarters, Brown and Johnson ; half back, Gleave, (captain); forwards, Evans, Beasley, J Burgess, and Lomas. The chemicals had an easy task in vanquishing their oisponents, running up a score of 1 goal, 3 tries, and four minors to one minor, in the twenty minutes that was played—ten min- utes each way. A team selected by H C Speakman, of Run- corn P.C. should have met a team of Wigan F.C. captained by Slavin, but the latter did not turn up and the former had therefore a walk over. St Helens F.C. alto scratched to a team of Warrington F.C. captained by Thomas Davies and the later had therefore to go through the farce of kicking a goal. Widnes Recreation then met Litherland and a most evenly contested game was the result. Litherland were eventually declared the victors by one try and one minor to 2 minors. Teams: Litherland ; full back, T Houghton ; three quarters, R me, J mime; half back, D Donaldson ; forwardsa Holme, W Houghton, W Johnson, T Singleton. Recreation : full bac'k, T. Wilkiuson ; three quarters, J Smith and H Boardman; half back, David McCririe; for- wards. T Whelan, R Charles, J Wright, and E Gordon. QUARTER-MILE FLAT RACE HANDIC#I.-let prize silver cop (pr«sented by F. H. Gossage, Esq ) ; 2ad, case of salts and muffins, value £2 2; 3rd prize, cigarette case, value £1 is. There were eight started for this popular event. Morris. of Widnes Gymnasium Harriers, was on the scratch mark, and the race, as anticipated, lay between that well. known runner and J B Farr am, of Widnes C.C., who was receiving 27 yards start. Morris passed his man in grand style, mad on reaching Farram in the straight a close stroogle ensued, Morris eventually coming in a winner by about a foot. F Wareing, St Helens F.C., was is good third. Result : I, S Morris ; 2ad, .1 B Farram ; •3rd, F Wareing. _ . _

'IWO MILES BICYCLE HANDICAP—Iet prize, oak•monn- teel inkstand and gong, value .£5 5s ; 2nd, biscuit box, value .£2 2s : 3rd prize, eilver whistle and match box, value £1 Is. There were 12 entries for this event, and eight started. C E Stoker, of Anfield RC., occupying the scratch position whilst J H Handler, of Widnes 13. C., was limit man with 300 yards start. One by one the men fell out until only f ur were left, and Stoker giving up in the last lap left the three placed to finish. The winner rode a capital race. 1, R E Garrett, Leys B C. (200 yards) ; 2, J B Webster, War- rington H. (110) ; 3, F 1 Allen, Warrington C.C. (250 yds.) Fifty yards separated first and second. ONE MILE FLAT RACE HANDICAP.—For this event there were IS entries, and 14 competitors toed their respective marks. Early in the race F Franklin, of Widnes, dropped out, and made a complaint that J Massey, of Warrington, had interfered with him, and various other incidents in the race raised the antagonism of the spectators. Corning into the straieht for home, G Etheridge.(Farnworth F.C.) and J Clarke (Widnes A.F.C.) were respectively first and eeerind, whilst Massey, running very strongly, was third. Massey, was, however, not coming in quick enough for his partisans, and G. Raton& (Warrington), who had retired at a pre- vious stage in the race, jumped into the track, and ran with Massey to make a pace. A constable at once interfered, and the spectators lx,-oke through the barriers, and a scene of great confusion ensued. Feeling against Massey ran very high, and be was unable to complete the course, but Etheridge and Clarke succeeded in passing the tape. The jadges reserved theit decision until next day. SATURDAY.

The sports were continued Or; Saturday afternoon in the Show Field, Parnworth. Fine weather again prevailed, and there were pveral thousands of spectators present. The grand stand WAS well occupied by the ladies of the district. The programme contained 31 events, and some excellent snort was witnessed. The principal pedestrian present was Wharton, of Darlington College, the goal keeper to the celebrated Preston North End Football Club. He arrived too late for his heat in the 120 yards handicap, but the committee kindly made up a heat of other late arrivals, and Wharton won easily. In the trial heat, however, hc could not secure a place. He was, however, conceding ten yards to the winner. Later in the afternoon he made amends by easily Carrying off the first piize in the 100 yards scratch race. He was also placed first for the quarter mile scratch race, but be appeared to he pumped out at the finish. For the mile scratch race Pitchford, of Liverpool Gymnasium, was a general favourite, but Parry, of Salford, made the running from the start, and won the event with astonishing eat,. Before passing the tape, Pitchford pulled up to put on his coat. and Shay, who had been at least 50 yards be- passed him and was placed second. A doubt was thrown upon Parry's bona files, but the suggestion was afterwards withdrawn, and an apology tendered and ac- cepted. The two fought their battle over again in the half mile flat race, Pitchford defeating Parry by about three yards. There was some capital racing in the 220 yards handicap, which was run in six heats, the winner ultimately turning up in H. Feay, of Manchester. W. Riley, of Run- corn, ran Stott, of Rock Ferry, who had second honours, a very close race in the beat, the young footballer only sue- c,innhifig to the extent of about half a foot. Two of the prettiest spectacles of the afternoon were the half n.ile handicap, for which no less than 25 competed, and the mile handicap, for which there were 21 runners. A local man in J. Kelly. of St. Mary's RC., managed to secure third place in the latter event There was a splendid race for the one mile bicycle handicap, J. Graham, of Sefton and Dingle 8.C., formerly of Runcorn, winning in fine style. In the three miles competition he had to be content with third place. .1. B. Webster, of Warrington, took the lead after three-quarters of a mile had been traversed, and never being again headed, won in handsome fashion, and he was greeted with a hearty cheer. Great interest was taken in the football contests, a feature introducod this year for the first time, in place of the steeplecbse and the high jumping. The rivalry between the teams was very keen, and the play was somewhattrough in consequence. The violence in the Warrington v. Wid• nes match was very marked, but the rougher the display the greater appeared to be the delight of the spectators. who gave forth a tremendous cheer when Widnes walked off the field victors by four minor points te one after play- ing an extra ten minutes. Each member of the winning team received a handsome gold medal valued at £2 23, and the runners up were presented with silver medals of a simi- lar pattern. It is pleasing to record that the sports passed off very smoothly throughout, there being no repetition of the clis.;raceful scene th a occurred on the previous even- ing. Betting was no doubt the cause of that fiasco, but on Saturday afternoon there were prominently displayed in various parts of the grounds notices "No betting allowed." Oembling was, however, still carried on, but not to so great an extra as formerly, and the " pencillers" gave out the odds te 2 to 1 on the field," &c., in very low and mild terms, instead of in their usual stentorian fashion. The pleasure of the visitors was much enhanced through the perform- ances of the Widnes Soap Works brass band, under the conductorship of Mr. William Jennett. Details:—

div.head: JUBILEE.
div.p: THE JUBILEE.
A STATE PAGEANT.

Her Majesty the Queen, it is announced, has been directed in her consideration of the ceremonial to be observed at Westminster Abbey on the 21st inst. by a desire to give her subjects the full benefit of a State ceremonial. Semi-State will be the authorised name given to the proceedings, but the pageant will have a magnificence such as has not been seen in London since the Coronation. The Queen will have a seat in the last State carriage, which will be appurtenanced,by all the trappings of full State, with the exception of a arrive roof. The cream-coloured ponies, with royal purple and crimson morocco harness, only used upon very leaportant occasions, will draw the open carriage which contains the •sovereign. At least twelve carriages conveying Royalty and princely guests will precede, the six nearest her Majesty in front being of the same style of grandeur to that of the Queen's equipage. Mounted guards of honour will be detailed by the War Office to accompany the Kings and Queens and the next heirs to thrones of Europe in the procession, and foot guards of honour will be pofted to salute them as they pass. The Queen will wear, as usual, her mourning, which, as a symbol of grief for the death of her Consort, she has never thrown off; but as the occasion,is of special gratification, not only to herself, but to all her people, the sombreness of her costume will be broken by the colours of the ribbons of the greater orders of which she has been the recipient from foreign States and by the ribbons of our own great orders. All the ladies in her Majesty's cortege will likewise appear with their orders upon their shoulders, but their dress will be of a more enlivening colour, and will be set off by the Kings' and Princes' costumes, which will be of full State or levee dress. It has not yet been finally decided who will ride in the carriage with the Sovereign, but the Crown Princess of Prussia (the Princess Royal) will certainly be in a prominent place. Of the military display upon the occasion we can only say that it will be beyond, both in scope and magnificence, anything ever seen before. Nearly ten thousand men of every arm of the service will be, present along the route, it being the Queen's special desire that every branch of the services should be represented. Cavalry, artillery, infantry, Royal Marines, and able-bodied seamen will represent the regular forces, while ,the volunteers and militia will prominently figure in connection with the auxiliary force. The disp.-,sition of the troops closing the two miles of roadways her Majesty will travel has not vet been decided, but it has been fixed that the Guards, the flower of the British army," and the Blue Jackets, the stalwarts of our coast, will form the prin- cipal guards of honour both at Buckingham Palace and at Weatminster Abbey, detachments of each service being drawn up 100 strong on each side of the road- way at the point where the Queen emerges from Buckingham Palace, and where she alights at the Abbey. There will be a large number of bands at points along the route. The bunting display will be of great magnificence, especially at Piccadilly Circus, where flags will be festooned from the centre to the outside pf the circle in the form of a huge umbrella tent; and at Parliament-stseet, again, there will be a most unique display, particularly on the house fronts. Of the Abbey itself it may be said that Mr. Taylor, of the Office of Works, who is chiefly responsible for the work, has carried out the erection of seats. Some 9,500 seats are available upon the huge but not unsightly tiers of gallieries which on every side are seen. Immediately under the lantern is the Queen's dais, or State pew, raised above the main floor of the building a few feet, and here in the old Coronation chair, and surrounded by 32 members of her own Royal blood, the Queen will return thanks for her 50 years' reign. Within the altar rails in front of the dais and close to the Communion table will be seated 16 Kings and Queens and next heirs to the thrones of Europe. On the right of the Queen will stand Peers, and on the left members of the House of Com- mons. The service will last about three quarters of an hour, when her Majesty will leave. '`

div.head: CURRENT POLITICS.
div.p: CURRENT POLITICS.

Mr. John Dillon, M.P., speaking at a meeting near Leicester, on Saturday, said the Crimes Bill would pro- hibit free speech in Ireland and the liberty of the press. Irishman had nothinglo thank Parliament for but Coer- cion Bills.

Lord Hartington has written to Mr. Boxer, Kiddermin- ster, acknowledging a resolution passed by the Gordon Habitation of the Primrose League relative to the Irish question. His lordship says he is gratified to observe, from the terms of the resolution, that the meeting re- cognised the fact tint the supporters of the Government are actuated by a desire to suppress lawlessness, and to deal with the whole Irish question in a spirit of fairness and liberality. Mr. Gladstone has addressed the following letter to Mr. Bright :—" Dellis Hill, June 11th, 1887.—My dear Bright,—Having my attention called by many corres- pondents to your letter of the Bth inst., and always re- garding you as a good and kind friend, I write to apprise you that you have inadvertently fallen into an error of fact when, as you say, I spoke as if there were no province of Ulster. In that same speech, referring to the essentials of the Irish Government Bill, I spoke expressly of Ulster, as you will find by reference to any report of tolerable accuracy.—Yours sincerely, W. E. GLADSTONE."

At the Atmual dinner of the Cambridge Carlton Club on Saturday, the Duke of Abercorn, responding for the House of Lords, said that Mr. Smith's motion for curtail- ing prolonged debates in the Lower House would be supported 'by the country. If the Crimes Rill became law, ancrwas efficiently worked, a vast amount of crime in Ireland would disappear. Sir Richard Webster said the Conservative cause never looked brighter thhn now. It was clear if Mr. Gladstone's reasoning in South Wales was to be carried to its logical conclusion, that there must be Home Rule for Wales, Scotland, and Ireland. They were determined, however, to maintain the supre- macy of Parliament over the whole of the United King- dom. •

The bill introduced into the present session of Parlia- ment by Mr. Burdett-Coutts, Sir Henry Selwin-Ibbetson, Mr. C. A. Whitmore, Mr. Howard Vincent, Lord Claud Hamilton, and Colonel Laurie, to remove the disabilities of the police, has, with the assistance of the Govern- ment, passed into law, and takes effect at once. All police officers and constables will now be en- titled to have their names; placed upon the register of voters, and to vote either in the capacity of householders, lodgers, or under the service fran- chise, according to their respective qualifications. It will be the duty of the overseers to insert the names of all police officers entitled to be enrolled in respect of the occupation of any dwelling-house in their lists, published on the Ist of August next, and also those who are entitled under what is known as the service franchise. This work would be greatly facilitated if the superin- tendents at the local police stations in county and, borotigh divisions would forward the names and ad.- dresses of the members of their force to the overseers ah' once. Those of the police entitled under the lodger; franchise will have to claim to be placed on the lodgerl register of voters on or before the 20th of August next.

IRELAND. It is stated that an interview between Mr. Studdert, agent for the Vandeleur estates, West Clare, and several priests took place at Kilrush on Saturday. The latter, on behalf of the tenants, against whom evictions are pending, made &nal offers of settlement, the terms being 35 per cent rent reduction on the old rents. and 20 per cent on the judicial rent, and the agent undertook to forward the proposals to Captain Vandeleur.

i An application was made before Judge Boyd in the Irish liandCourt at Dublin, on Monday, to make absolute a conditional order to attach the Rev. Arthur Divine, P.P., tallaghadereen, County Sligo, for contempt of court in advising tenants on the Taaffe estate in County ~Mayo to adopt the "Plan of Campaign." The applica- ,ftion was granted. Affidavits were made by the rev. J gentleman and two of the tenants denying positively j that he had advised the adoption of the "Plan of Corn- paign " or interfered to prevent the payment of rent. I A Banturk telegram states that the house of Bartholo- mew Curtin, farmer, near Rockchapel, has been visited by a dozen or more men, masked and armed. After they had, fired several shots through the windows, they demanded to see the son, John Curtin, who Was seized and beaten. The father intervened, and young Curtin fled, but a shot was fired after him, and he was struck on the right side of the head, and is in, a critical state. Various reasons are given for the outrage. Some state that it was agrarian, while others declare that it was the , result of a family quarrel. A labourer named Hurley, who was one of several persons arrested in connection with the murder of a farmer, named Rahilly, near Killarney, years ago, was shot dead in the house of a widow named Burke, at Pines, at about half-past ten on Monday night, twelve shots being fired at him in succession. Burke, the widow's husband, to whom Hurley had been labourer, was found dead under his Own cart and within view of his own house, about four months back. Since then, Hurley has remained in the widow's house; but the friends of Burke entertained ill-feelings towards him, as they_ suspe.cted that he was the murderer of Burke.

THE BODYKE EVICTIONS. • The Press Association correspondent telegraphs from Bodyke:—The reply of Colonel King-Harman in the House of Commons to Mr. Conybeare's question regard- ing the alleged batoning of Pat Walsh's mother is much discussed here. I was present when the old woman was carried out of the house. She certainly bore the marks of recent ill-usage, and declared that a constable had struck her on the forehead with his baton. Her , daughters corroborated .this. There were two black marks, one on her left temple and another on the cheek, such as would be produced by a blunt instrument; and the. old woman's face subsequently became swollen from the effects of the wounds. The affair at Feakle on Sunday is still the topic of conversation throughout the district Dr. Donworth, of Bodyke, who has been attend- ing nine persons from scalp wounds in Feakle and the district, states that the boy Purcell, who is suffering from a scalp wound two inches long, is rather better, but that , the man Ryan, whose head was a mass of wounds, was in a serious condition prom the danger of erysipelas I supervening. Two constables were takes into Limerick from injuries from stones, and they remain at the LhosciitaL .

div.head: PRINCE ALBERT VICTOR'S VISIT.
div.p: PRINCE ALBERT VICTOR'S VISIT.

On the occasion of the visit to Ireland of Prince Albert Victor of Wales, who will represent the Queen at the Jubilee celebrations in Dublin, the following will be the leading events in the programme :—His Royal Highness will arrive by special steamer at Kingstown at 4 30 on the 27th inst., and will receive and reply to an address Proceeding to Dublin another address will be presented. From the railway station the Prince will drive to the Viceregal Lodge, and subsequently dine with the judges and leaders of the bar at the King's Dine. In the evening the Prince will attend the citizens' ball in Lemster Hall. On Tuesday morning more addresses will be presented, and at noon there will be a military review in Phcenix Park. In the afternoon the Prince and Viceregal party will attend the Jubilee thanksgiving service in St. Patrick's Cathedral, when Lord Plunkett (the Lord Primate) and some ot the bishops will officiate. After the service the Prince will be installed as Knight of St. Patrick in St.. Patrick's Hall and in the evening there will be a grand banquet of the Knights of St. Patrick and other noblemen'. In addition to the above ceremonies, his Royal Highness will laf the foundation stone of the new wing of the hospital for incurables at Donnybrook, and will "end a garden party given by Prince Edward of Saxe-Weamar.

Lake, of the Fleece Inn, Lymm.—ln both cases the applicants were refereed to the Altrincham sessions, on Monday, the bench declaring tiaat if the Altrincharn bench were willing to allow exten- sions in their part of the division, the Lymm bench would would also agree to do so in the cases of the applicants.

DEIINKENNESS —Hannah-Harrison, for being drunk and disorderly. in Gilbert Street, on the 3rd June was fined 101 and costs 8s 61 or 14 days bard labour.—Daniel Owen. a stranger, for being drunk and incapable, in Mill.street, on the 11th inst., was fined 5s and costs 8s 6d.

MONDAY.--Before Mr. Holbrook Haskell, junr. and Mr.

H. W. Deacon. DIMNIC AND DISORDEELY.—Stephen Scatty an old offen- der was charged with being drink and disorderly, in Water- loo-road, on Saturday night and also with wilfully e.mag- ing the cell in which he was placed. He was ordered to pay or go to gaol for 14 days.—Peter Sinnott and Edward Showan, were each fined 53 god costs for drunkenness.— Owen Lewis, for committing a breach of the peace, in War- rington-road, on Saturday night, was bound over to ba of good behaviour for 3 months —James Nolan, of Birkenhead was convicted of sleeping in an empty dwelling-house in Albert-road, on Sunday morning, was sentenced to 7 day. hard labour.

As the boy bay- ing been in custody since B,itivd ly, the Magistrates after recording a conviction against him wrdered his discharge.

GENERAL NEWS.
John Luitton, an old man was arrested at B water, on Saturday night, charged with kicking hi=. to death.

The Duke of Norfolk has been appointed a member ot the Royal Commission on Education, in place of Mz. Molloy, M.P., who resigned. SUNDAY OPENING OF A Fa.las LuntsaT.—The terror Library and Art Museum Committee of the Bradford Car, ppration has passed a resolution recommending the Town Council to make the past temporary arrangentesst: for opening the Free Library on Sunday afternoons per— manent.

The amount of British money embarked in Colon* investments and securities is increasing' very rapiilar. At the end of 1833 it was put at £620,000,000, and Au, now estimated to exceed £744,000,000, or nearly as much, as the National Debt, and in excess of the country's; foreign investments.

On Saturday afternoon an explosion occurred at 4he ammunition factory of Messrs. Dyer and Robson:Wool— wich-road, East Greenwich. In the shed where that explosion took place, two women cngaged in making cartridges were severely injured, and two others sligttlr burned. The shed was severely damaged.

A brutal prize fight took place early on Momlay it the outskirts of Northampton, between two local light weights, known as Tunk and Buck. The battlA was of' the gamest description. Twenty-four rounds had been., fought before Buck, who hitherto had had the worst of it, landed Tunk a terrible blow over the heart, which so stunned him that his second threw up the sponge,. Both men were badly bruised. Many spectators were present. At a largely representative meeting of chainmakers at Cradley Beath, on Monday afternoon, it was stated that the strike for an advance of wages had now lasted tea months, and as sections of the employers were deter- mined not to concede the advance, the only remedy was co-operation. Gentlemen who were willing to float the, scheme had sent a cheque for £5O for the relief fund. n. was decided to take all the necessary steps to forna co-operative society and provide works in the district.

SITICIDE OF A LIVERPOOL STOCKEROKER.—Considerable sensation was caused on Liverpool Stock Exchange, ea, Monday, by the announcement that Mr. Hobbs. senior partner in the stockbroking firm of Hobbs and Stitt, had that morning emomitted suicide by shooting hirnselt through the head with a revolver. The shocking occur- rence took place in Waterloo Park, near the deceased's. residence. Deceased had been depressed for some time. but he had no tnancial difficulties. The deceased'a former partner shot himself nine years ago.

THE FALSE MARKING OF GOODS.—The House of COOO- - Select Committee on the Mercb and ise Marks Bill sat again on Monday. Mr. J. H. Lees, managing director of the firm of Messrs. A. and A. Crompton and Co., calm spinners, Shaw, gave evidence confirmatory of that , given by Mr. George Lord as to the faige reeling and marking of cotton yarns; and Mr. Councillor tittley, ot Sheffield, gave further evidence as to the feeling of Uri Sheffield workmen on fradulent marking. The evidenco 4- being concluded, the committee will consider their repOrt.

• A FARMER GOURD To Darrn.—OnMonday a sad affair. happened at Mixenden, near Halifax. A farmer name& Thomas Greenwood, of The Height, Mixenden, went out to see after his cattle, which were in a field beyond 11E1 house, and did not return as usual. Later on a neigh- bouring farmer named Jnshua Ingham found the maul lying in one of the fields dead, he having been gored b 7. his own bull. The bull was previously known to be. dangerous. Deceased, who was about 60 years, leaves widow and several children.

GARIDALDIANS AND THE DUKE OF SUTHERLAND.—On Fri-t • day morning a deputation of Garibaldians waited upon' the Duke and Duchess of Sutherland at Stafford House., and presented to them, on behalf of the 'Thousand of Marsala, two gold medals and an address commemorat- ing the landing at Marsala. The Duke and Duchess re- , plied to the address, and charged the deputation to convey I- to those whom they represented the expression of theirk-. entire sympathy with the cause of Italian progress and': liberty. The result of a record kept for five years ending with February, 1887, of the suicides in the United States, has t, been published. The suicides thus brought to notice number 8,226. No alarming increase is to be perceived year by year if exception is made of the unusually heavy ' list-1,943—0f last year. The average for the period r gives about 1,645 to each year. The statistics seern te show conclusively that summer is the season when suicides are the most frequent. As regards the months, , June shows the largest list and February the smallest, THE Kgwrisn TRAGEDY.—The remains of Florence Rate Poysden, who was cruelly murdered by Charles , Walter, farm servant, were interred in Teynhat. Church- - - yard, near Faversham, on Saturday afternoon. Upwards t of 200 residents of surrounding villages witnessed the - solemn ceremony. Besides relatives, several of the Sun- day school children, among whom deceased was a favourite, followed, and afterwards sang over the grave.l, The coffin was covered with wreaths. The mother of deceased was too ill to attend the funeral. 1 RECKLESSNESS BY COLLIERS.-.-AL WhiLehaVeD, On Mon- day, James Avery, miner, was summoned for unlocking a safety lamp, and George Armstrong, miner, was sum- moned for having lucifer matches, tobacco, and a pipe, with him in the Walk Mill Colliery, the property of the, Moresby Colliery Company. The men's clothes were, searched in consequence of the serious explosion which'. recently occurred, and where matches were found on the, . bodies of the men killed. Armstrong was fined £2, or one month's imprisonment. A warrant was granted fort the apprehension of Avery, who did not appear. EXTRAORDINARY PROCEEDINGS AT A FlRM—Damage toi the extent of £12,000 was caused by a fire at Ayr late on i Saturday night. The fire originated in a draper's shop,. the window of which was hung with highly inflammable, . material and lighted by gas. The assistants escaped:' with difficulty, and several children had to be hastily' removed. Amongst the buildings destroyed was the. Eagle Tavern, and many persons became intoxicated with the liquor which they stole therefrom. Several persons were apprediendeclin the act of carrying off some barrels of beers.

TECHNICAL AND COMMERCIAL EDUCAT/ON.—A privati! meeting of members of Parliament and others was held at the House of Commons on Monday for the purpose of ` making arrangements for the establishment of a national association for the promotion of technical and commcr- • cial education. Lord Hartington presided, and there, were also present the Marquis of Ripon, Sir John Lub- - • bock, Professor Huxley,, Mr. Mundella, Sir Lyon Playtair,,, kc. Resolutions in adoption of a scheme were pa.ssed, and a Provisional Executive Committee was appointed ' to take steps for the organisation of the association.

MR. GLADSTONE A.ND vEx Sotictrott-Grsinat..—An ex- tract from a report of a speech by the Solicitor-General at Salisbury on Friday week living been forwarded?" to Mr. Gladstone, the right hon. gentleman has sent the. following reply:—" The two assertions imputed to the.. Solicitor-General are unfounded assertions. I never said ' Parliament ought to pass a Coercion Bill when the ' Government demanded it. I never suggested nor en- couraged obstruction, but have repeatedly endeavoured . to assist the Government in the conduct of a business which they have shown themselves so incompetent to . manage." Two Cnn.unsx Duowarxh.—A sad accident occurred: on Saturday in the Abbey Palk, Leicester. It appears that about noon an alarm was raised that two children had fallen, into the river Soar, opposite the Pavilion. The., drags were at once fetched, and within two hours the bodies of both children were drawn from the water. One was identified as Ernest Ross, ten years old, of Heanor-• street, and the other as George Moore, aged five years, of Denman-street. Nobody apparently saw them fall into the water, but it is supposed that they were playing on the bank and rolled "down the slope. Tax TRAGEDY IN LIVERPOOL.—The funeral of the three children murdered by their mother, Mrs. Anthony, at Walton, near Liverpool, took place on Sunday. Wyatt- street, the scene of the tragedy, was crowded by over 2,000 people. The shells were placed in an ordinary' hearse, and consisted of the baby, seven months old, the murdered girl Annie, and that of the boy Alfred. The father followed as chief nulurner, and seemed heart- broken by the terrible calamity. On arrival at the Kirk- dale Cemetery, a vast multitude met the procession. The Church of England service was read at the grave, and the, coffins were covered with wreaths and flowers.
