div.head: EXAMINER,
div.p: THE EXAMINER,
SATURDAY. JUNE 18, 1887.

THE Manchester Ship Canal Bill is having a somewhat hard time of it at the hands of Parliament; but we are pretty confident that it will survive the latest, and, let us hope, the last struggle for existence. It is galling to think that opponents who have been beaten so often should again have a chance of making themselves troublesome ; but they are net to have it all their own way— they ale limited alike as to time and as to mode of attack. It is quite right for Parlia- ment to make due inquiry as to the grounds of the proposal to issue preference stock, par- ticularly when, on the face of it, the House, as Mr. SCLATER-BOOTH stated, was being asked "to pass by the previous consent of the existing shareholders in the undertaking." If there were any reason to believe that the promoters of the scheme were taking advant- age of the occasion to play into the hands of financiers, at the expense of the original applicants for shares, Parliament would be -quite justified in refusing its assent to the new proposals; but such is not the case. Mr. Hormnswon=ral was in a position to show that, in making the new departure as to pre ference shares, the promoters were frilly com- plying 'with the spirit, if not the letter of the %law. Circulars have been sent to shareholders asking their •consent to the issue‘ of prefer- ence stock, and 'within a few days not less than 70 per cent of the applicants for shares gave their content to the application to Par- liament. No more than a half per cent ex- pressed their dissent; and such an impetus was immediately given to the movement that the new applications for shares have been treble the number of those held by the dissen- tients. With regard to the public bodies whose interests are at stake, namely, the London and North-Western Railway Company, the Mersey Dock Board, and •the Liverpool Corporation, they are warranted in seeing to it that no change is made which will result in the undertaking being less kona fide in its I character. They are credited in some quar- ters with desiring, from purely selfish mo- tives, that the whole undertaking shall collapse. but they cannot lay a view of this kind before the House of Ccimmons. They can, however, demand that nothing shall be done to jeopar- dise their interests; and as to this they are . being oonsiderately taken into account. The Ship Canal sill, at the suggestion of Mr. COURTNEY (chairman of Committees) was referred, on Manday. to a Special Committee of four; but the only point that they will be called upon to consider is whether the sub- stitution of the proposal to raise four millions of the capital by preference stock, and four millions by Grdinary stock is one that can be sanctioned, having regard to the •motive and purpose of the original arrangement. The opposition can be heard ora this point; but they will not be permitted to kill the bill by becoming, as BYRON has it, " internainable not eternal speakers." There has been too much of this game in the past, and so. to put a check on it, Sir HENRY JAMES, on Tuesday. moved that it be an instruction to the Com- mittee to report the bill to the House not later than the z+th June. Mr. COURTNEY thought it undesirable to hamper the commit- mittee with snch a restriction until it was seen whether time was being wasted; but it was forcib); urged by Mr. J. MACLEAN that if proceedit gs to limit the Committee were Laken after it had commenced operations, the

members of the Committee would look upon such action as a vote of censure. It was pointed out in the course of the discussion that the Committee could not be struck till the 23rd June, upon which Sir HENRY JAMES substituted Friday, the z7th June, as the date for the Committee to report to the House, thus leaving- three full days for the inquiry. Mr. SMITH, however, on behalf of the Ministry, opposed the motiv.i; and it ought to be put on ,record that a Tory Go- vernment at the 1a.4 moment sought to block the progress of the Ship Canal Bill. Mr. MUNDELLA, replying to Mr. SMITH, per- tinently observed that the persistent opposi- tion to which the bill had been subjected was a great scandal, which was to say that it was a scandalous thing for the Ministry to lend its influence to the opponents of the measure. Happily the Government were subjected in the matter to a most humiliating defeat ; for on Sir HENRY JAMES'S motion being submit- ted to a division it was found that there were 2+3 in its favour and 82 only against it. The Bill will therefore be reported to the House of Commons by the 271 h jest; but it will not even then be wholly out of danger. It will have to go before the House of Lords ; and, if there should be contention in the Upper House as to matters of form, much mischief may be caused by further delay. The whole project falls through if the requisite capital be not subscribed by the 7th August next ; and August will soon be here. Meantime the promoters are acting wisely in making arrangements in faith ; and there is every reason to believe that the preference shares will be subscribed directly after the assent of Parliament is obtained. It is now a race against time, but we believe the Ship Canal Company will win in the race.

HALF-TIMERS are evidently uncl:g the ban at some of the schools of Warrington, and Councillor PLATT has done good service in calling attention to the matter. It will be a surprise to most of the inhabitants, as it is to us, to learn that half-timers are, in many cases, charged double fees. They attend school half the day only, and yet they are called upon to pay extra! The practice is simply abominable, and school managers will do well to see to it that for the future no such charge can be brought against the schc ols with which they are connected. The law makes special provision for half-timers ; they are a recognised branch of the educational system and neither school teachers nor school managers are justified in raising the tariff against them. Councillor FRANCOMB is quite right in saving that the responsibility for action of this kind rests with the mana- gers rather than the teachers ; and pr:rhaps he is right, too, in stating that " in many schools there is great objection to half- timers because they are not dressed as well and kept as clean as those who attended full time." Granted that this is so, can it be said that considerations of this kind are to determine the difference between single and double fees ? Is it to be argued that the struggling mother who is too poor to dress her child well shall be•called upon to pay more in the shape of school fees than her well-to- do neighbour? Or, because a lad, having been half a day at work, goes to school in the afternoon with the smell of the workshop about him, is he to be called upon to pay more for a half-day's schooling than his play- mate who gets a full day's schooling ? 'To mention such a thing is to expose it to ridi- cule. The system of compulsory education was brought into operation as a means of reaching all classes, and the nation pays two- thirds of the cost of educating each child in our elementary schools, nct that the children of the poor may be placed 2.t a disadvantage, but that they may stand on a footing of equal- ity in our national schools. It is dishearten- ing —nay, it is inhuman—to tell "a widow with six children," who is honestly striving to make ends meet by sending one child to work as a half-timer, that because the child goes to school half-time she must pay extra for tuition. It is not to the point to say it is "unfair both to the schoolmaster and to the child " to require that full-timers and half- timers shall pass the same examination; for, if this be so, how much more unfair is it to the half-timer to ask him to pay for two loaves when he receives half a loaf only? Nor is it any more to the point to plead that half-timers have a tendency to lessen the grant. The grant is based upon a system which includes half-timers, who constitute a large per - centage of many Lancashire schools. If there are few half-timers in Warrington, let school mangers be thankful that they are in a better position than are their fellow managers in some other places, and act fairly as between child and child. There seems to be an impression abroad that the School Attendance Commit- tee have no means of remedying the griev- ance ; but we venture to suggest that if they will deal with each case as it arises, and make the matter public, school teachers and school managers will soon be shamed into doing the right thing. If they were still obdurate, an appeal could be made to the Education DcpartMent. We are much mistaken if their lordships would not interfere to put a stop to a practice which is utterly at variance with the plinciples upon which grants are made from the national exchequer in support of national education.

div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JUNE 18. 1887.
"TOUCH AND GO."

Beacon fires are all the go for next week; but bacon fires would suit some people better —judging from their hungry look. The weather has been hot—very hot. Our " P.D.," who has a knowledze of these things, says they have been having the lid off at a place which shall be nameless.

It has been decided that the Queen shall wear—not the crown in the Jubilee proces- sion, but a bonnet of "the finest point d'Alencon, with a front of black velvet form- ing a sort of coronet." It is being specially made for the occasion. We knew it was safe to bet on the bonnet.

Now that everybody has subscribed to celebrate the Queen's Jubilee, people are beginning to ask—What will ,her Majesty do to signalise the event ? She is not without the means to do the thing in royal style, and who will say that she is lacking in the will ? " Let us bide a wee," and we shall see what we shall see.
It was an Irishman who said he couldn't be in two places at once—" unless he were a bird." The Prince of Wales gets somewhere

near it on Tuesday, besides- attending the ball at the Reform Club, he presided at the Middle Temple as treasurer, and was at an assembly at the Foreign Office. But the Prince always was a lively bird.

Two colliers have had to be fined this week —one at Haydock and the other at Prescot— for such negligence in complying with the law as might have led in each case to a fatal mis- hap. Magistrates are justified in being severe in such cases. Workmen ought not to be permitted to endanger their own lives— to say nothing of the lives of other men.

Two young fellows, named Dolan and Moran, took to fighting. on Sunday, off Orford-road, Warrington, surrounded by a large crowd. The weather being "cold '—it was about 8o in the shade—'.hev resorted to this method of warming each other. When the thermometer rises to ion or izo, they will, of course, behave in a different fashion.

It is reported that Llrd Crawford's copy of the Mazarin Bible, obtained for ltss than £7OO, was sold to M. Quaritch, on Wednes- day, for £2,650. One would have thought M. Quaritch knew better than to give £2,650 for the first Bible printed from moveable types, when he can have the last Bible printed—all nice and clean—for tenpence.

Mr. Smith is out of his depth as leader of the House of Commons. He floundered shockingly on Tuesday in the matter of the Ship Canal Bill. He has applied the closure to the Nationalists in order to get the Coer- cion Bill passed; but closure to ensure thtt the Ship Canal Bill shall not fail—that would never do. Poor Mr. Smith! He led his fol- lowers into a queer .corner, and was badly beatem

The Corporation of London is in bad odour. Petitions have been got up in favour of the Coal and Wine dues, signatures being paid for—and no questions asked—at the rate of from 3s to 6s per hundred. One canvasser admits that he forged 1,600 names. But Parliament is not to be imposed on, and action is to be taken in the matter. The Corporation of London should be cut down; it cumbers the ground.

P.C. Sutton. of Runcorn, bade a seaman whom he found on the footpath "move on." A move was made, but it resulted in the officer being struck on the chest, and his clothes being torn. There is an old proverb which says that it is well to let sleeping dogs lie, and it would seem that it applies, too, to seamen. However, that seaman will probably lie in gaol for a few weeks. And , all through a nap which was followed by a rap.

That wall in front of the Warrineton Town Hall (and the Conservative Club) which had to come down is still." all there." The Jubi- lee Committee were willing, but the money "wouldn't run to it." Alderman Harrison, as a sort of after-thought, has tried the Town Council, but they will have none of it. Since nobody will find money for taking down the wall, how would it be to try a blast of trum- oetsl It succeeded in bringing a wall down at Jericho.

Mary Thompson, of St. Helens, seems to like the inside of a gaol. She is scarcely out of her teens, and yet she has been imprisoned no less than fifty-eight times., Her latest es- capade has been to break two plateglass windows, doing damage to the amount of .£7 She has been sent to prison for two months, and meantime she will have time to consider how to vary her performances so as to be made wholly happy by getting im- prisoned for life.

Mr. Chamberlain used to be logical and consistent; but he is ceasing to be either one or the other. Speaking at Willis's rooms the other evening, he said he could not see any hope of reconciliation with the Liberal party; and yet he went on to state that Mr. Glad- stone's bill "had been fißally abandoned by its author." If this be so, what more does he want ? Does he require that the policy shall be resumed as a means to reconcilia- tion? Mr. Chamberla:n has hob-nobbed with the Tories till he tall:A like one. "Evil communications corrupt goo 1 manners."

What a different example Mr. Gladstone sets bcrth as to manner and matter : Like the prophet of old, he says "Cone now and let us reason together ; " he appeals to the common sense and common feeling of hu- manity ; and, as in the case of Mr. Bright, he will not take offence at friend for offen- sive and unfriendly language. He knows that Mr. Bright is better than he paints him- self; and tries to win him over by "heaping coals of fire on his head." Meet him as to the principle of dome Rule, and he is open to any modification as to the method of carrying it out. He is, indeed, a grand old man.

Here is a capital story from " Truth :--- The solemn service was progressing in Win- chester Cathedral, and the dean sat en- throned,when a telegram WAS handed to him. He opened it, and cast , his eyes up to heaven in dire perplexity. = It ran thus, " Ormonde has won." Who was Ormonde ? and what had he won ? Vainly canons and such-like minor lights were consulted. If they knew they pretended not to. It was subsequently discovered that the telegram had been sent to Mr. Dean. a trainer at Winchester, but as it was addressed "Dean, Winchester," it was handed to the dean. The telegraph clerks were probably under the im- pression that this dignitary had put a trifle on the race, and had desired that the result should be at once forwarded to him.

FRVICIS HETES, OF WFDNES.—At St. Bede's Rohm Catholic Cnapel, Angleton. on Tuesday, Mr. Francis Efeyes, of Appleton. a member of ,he Widnes Local Board, was married to Miss JOS Johnson,.of Glad- stone-etreet, Widnes. Benjamin Griffiths, a powerfully. built man, was charged with assaulting an elderly man named William Welding. On the 10. h irist, Welding was passing across the waste grcund near the new, Catholic Chapel, when the defendant went up ta him, and, without the slightest provocation, struck him three times on the month, and knocked him to the ground. He then knelt upon his body, and tried to strangle him. Mr W B Linaker, solicitor. Runcorn, witnessed the defendant's brutal con- duct, and told Welding that if be summoned his aaaailant he would giveevidence for him, as he considered the assault was most cowardly, Mr Linaker gave evidence corrobora- tive of the above statement, and he was cordially thanked by Mr Muspratt for the part be bad taken in the matter. The defendant, who pleaded guilty, was fined Ll and costs, Ss 63, or a Tenth's hard labour. Bickford 23 16 20 10 69 SOCIETY FOR THE PROPAGLTIOX OF THE GOSPEL:— SERVICES At RUNCORN.—Sermons were preached on Sunday In the Runcorn Parish Church, at the Weston Paint, Wes- ton, and Newtown Churches in connection with the above society. The preachers at the Parish Church were the Revs. G. H. Smith, M.A, (formerly of AntranAnarivo. Madagaecar, in the morning and evening), and W. Bryant, 8.A., B.Sc. (in the afternoon) ; at Weston Point, the Revs. J. D. Ozanne, B.A. (in the morning), and A. Maitland Wood, .1.A., vicar of Runcorn (in the evening) ; at Wes- ton, the Revs. J. H. Wilcockson, 8.A., incumbent of Wes- ton Point (in the morning), G. A. Tindall, B.A. (in the afternoon), and W. Bryant (in the evening; at Newtown, the Revs. G. A. Tindall (in the morning), G. H. Smith (in the afternoon). and J. H. Wilcockson (in the evening.) The annual meeting was held on Monday evening in the Parish School, Runcorn, when the vicar, the Rev. A. Maitland Wood, presided. The Rev. l. H. Smith delivered an in- teresting address on the work of the society, which was listened to with mach pleasure. • WIDNES FREE LIDIURY Comm-cm—A meeting was held on Thursday afternoon, at the new Public Offices. Mr. H. Wale Deacon presided, and there were present Dr. O'Reeffe, Messrs. J. Fitzpatrick, F. H. Pankhurst, E. Cary, William Sadler, .1. Midwood, J. F. Allen (clerk), and Miss Procter (libearian.)--The Chairman gave the new members a hearty welcome, and expressed the hope that they would all work amicably together for the success of the library. (Hear, hear.) It was decided to hold the committee meet- ings on the second Friday in each month.—The Librarian reported that during the month of May 780 volumes bad been borrowed from the leading department and ,35 from the reference department. The numb-r of guarantee forms received during the same period was 374, for which cards had been issued. The cash received had amounted to £3 44 sd. includingr£2 14e 61 for sale of catalogie-s; 9s 3,1 sundries ; and 8.1 fines.—Accounts amounting to £92 2s were passed for payment. It was decided to close the library on Jubilee Day. WIDEEs ScwoOL BOARD. The monthly meeting was held on Tuesday, Mr. R. Bradshaw, the vice-cbairman, pre- siding. Present—the Very Rev. Dean Finegan, the 219 V. George Bond, the Rev. J. Clarke Messrs. R. H. Davies, H. W. Deacon. 1. B. Jellison, J. W. Wareing, Dr. O'Keeffe. and G. H. Denby (clerk.)—Tbe minutes of the District Educa- tion Committee, adopted on the motion of Mr. Deacon, stated that eluring May there were 65 applications for the payment of school fees, which were recommended to he paid in 69 Cases. There appeared before the committee 194 per- sons for contravention of the Education Act, and 34 were Prosecuted and, convicted before the magistrates. It PM recommended • that after eight year's service the salary of the school attendance officer, G. R. Joynson, be increased according to the scale of the Board.—On the recommenda- tion of the School Management Committee it was decided that the teachers be instructed not to receive any children from the ontside townships without the sanction of the &hoot Isnagement Committee. Accounts amounting to £572 2s 34 were passed for peyment. and the receipts for the month were stated at £1.56 3s 81—It was resolved that the next monthly meeting be held the first week in July and the following meeting on the last Tuesday in August. CORPUS CHRISTI PROCESSION AT DITTON COLLEGE.—On Sunday the aunnal open-air procession of the Blessed Sad- rament was mode from the beautiful church belonging to the college through the ample and picturesque grounds, and back to the church again. The sacred edifice was crowded to excess. The ceremony commenced with an act of repa- ration said before the high altar by the Rev. Father Connor, 8.3., who afterwards preached an earnest sermon on the words 't This is My body." Afterwards a procession of clergy filed into the sanctuary, about twelve being vested in copes or chasubles, and the remainder wearing surplices. There were also outside the chancel about twenty-five lay brothers, a number of school girls of tender years wreathed in white veils and carrying baskets of choice flowers, which they afterwards strewed before the Blessed Sacrament as it was carried in procession. This large company, after the "0 Saintaris” and other hyrnes had been sung, slowly filed out of the church into the grounds. the Host, enclosed within a monstrance, being carried ET the Most Rev. Father Lohman, head of the German province of the Companions of Jesus, accompanied by the, Very Rev. Father Sky, as dea- con, and the Rev. Father Burkard. S.J , as sub.deacon. The procession included alsl the brass hand of th;> Widnes For- esters and about eighty members of the boys' modality con- nected with St. Francis Xavier's College, Liverpool, under ' the direction of Fathers Redman and Corrigan. The com- pany afterwards re-entered the church, when solemn bene- diction, was again given, and a number of hymns and chante, led by a choir of priests and port accompanied by the organ and partly by the brass inotruments, closed a stately function.

SUDDEN DEATH AT FARNWORTH.—Ed ward Athertnn, an old official of the Widnes Urea Board, who lived in Derby- road, Farnworth, was found dead in bed on Thursday morning. Deceased had suffered for a numbar of years from bronchitis, and had been attended by Dr. O'Neil. Before going to bed en Wednesday night he complained of herng unwell. An inquest will not be held. STABBING CASE AT WIDNES —At Widnes Police Court, yesterday, John l'alitebell, shoemaker, of Mersey-road, was charged with having unlawfully wounded Behert l‘tic Conachy, labourer, 71, Cburch•street. Prisoner and prose- ' cutor are relatod by marriage, and after drinking together, ',they quarrelled, and g.t to scuffling, during which the pri- soner stabbed prosecutor on the left arm with 3 pocket knife. A remand until Mon,lay W:t9 granted. A CAPTAIN ROBBED AT 11utticomq.—Francia Matthew 'Maloney, IS years of age, a seaman on board the Annie Conley was charged with stealing a eilver lever watch and seven foreign coins, the property of hia captain. The cap- tain was absent from the vessel on Sunday. On his return he missed the articles mentioned, and, suspecting the prisoner, accused him of the theft. Later the captain dis- covered that the watch had been replacd in his drawer, and PC. Dale then found the coins secreted in the prisoner's "bunk." The prisoner was sentenced to 21 day's hard labour. .

The Foresters' Club were holding their annual demonstration on that day, and in- tended to hold a ball in the eyening.—Mr Muspratt said it was a mistake to associate such an application with the Jubilee Day.—Permission was given to keep the house open until one o'clock. Hazlehurst, a seaman named Jobs Boyd was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Waterloo-road, the previous night. id also with assaulting P.C. Sutton, and damaging his uniform to the extent of ss. The prisoner was lying asleep on the footpath. and the constable awakened -him and told him to "move on" Instead of obeying, the man struck the officer on the chest, arid kicked him. Dur- ing the struggle that ensued the officer's clothing was torn. The prisoner was ordered to pay 37s 41, or go to gaol for five we•lrs. A RUNCORN WOMAN CHARGED WITH THEFT.—At Run- corn Petty Sessions, on Monday, Ann Key, a very respect- able looking woman, whose house is at 20, Wellington- street, was charged with stealing a tablecloth worth Es, the property of John Tonks. of High-street.—Mrs Tooke said she did not wish to prosecute the prisoner in any shape or form. The tablecloth was not stolen: it was given Mrs Key to wash.—ln answer to Superintendent Holliogwortb, Mrs Tooke said eh e did not tell Mrs Key to pledge the cloth. —Superintendent Hollingwinth remarked that the pawn- broker had given the woman in custody for pledging a , tablecloth marker' with the name of Tonks.—Acting upon the wish of Mrs Tonke, the Bench discharged tho prismer. On the night el the 4th ins., Mrs McNamara was standing in the door- t way of her house, when the prisoner, who had te-1 c4ved twit the slightest provocation, so far as the evidence I revealed, went up to the woman and struck her a savage blow on the left side of the forehead with a poker which be I had crncealtd behind him. Is answer to the charge, the pri- soner Hid he bad no recollection of having committed the offence. He had been ill and confined to bed for two years and on the Saturday he h.d had a drop of whiskev.—He was I committed to the quarter Sessions for trial. THE RUNCORN MAGISTRATES Ole " JUBILEE DRINK. The magisvates declined to grant the exten- sions iyar.,l far. • THE VEN. ARCHDEACON BARBER and the Rev. Canon Dodd have been selected to represent the clergy of Cheshire at the Jubilee service in West- minster Abbey on Tuesday next. % CHESHIRE AND THE JUBILEE.—PubIic celebra- tions in connection with the Jubilee have already begun in Cheshire by rejoicings at Malpas, where business was practically suspended. while the chil- dren and aged people enjoyed separate feasts. The occasion was also signalised at Middlewich, Che- shire, on Wednesday, by the formal presentation to , the town of a town hall, the gift of Colonel France- Hayhurst, of Bostock Hall. The building • was opeded and handed over to the tdwn for ever. BIRMINGHAM SHIP CANAL SCHEME.---A meeting of the Committee for the promotion of the Birming- ham Ship'Canal scheme was held on W4dnesday, Mr. P. Stanhope, M.P., presiding. It was reported that the probable cost of improving existing water- ways and purchasing existing property would be £2,000,000. It was estimated there would be from 500,000 to 750,000 tons of new traffic, which would yield an average toll of 2s per ton, or from £50,000 to £75,000 per annum. The Committee proposed to work the canal, which would run from Birmingham to the Bristol Channel. themselves. FREAK OF' NATUILE.—Many of our readers have seen or heard of the two-horned ponies which were exhibited at Croft last year, but another freak of nature may now be seen in the village, namely, a, cockerel, aged about nine months, with four legs. i It is a cross bred fowl, and is perfectly formed n the fore part of its body, with well-formed legs. Close behind them are two other legs protruding backwards. When the fowl sits down none of its legs are visible, and it has full use in them, except for walking. The fowl is quite healthy. It is sup- posed that the egg out of which it wits hatched was a double-yolked one. THE CANADIAN TARIFF ON IRON AND STEEL.—A telegram from Ottawa. dated Wednesday says: Sir Charles Tupper, Minister of Finance, has sub- mitted to the Dominion Parliament resolutions effecting changes in the tariff for iron and steel manufactures to meet the views of the British manufacturers. The chief changes are in boiler plate and sheet iron, common or black nails, and plates of iron or steel of sixteen gauge or thicker. On these the reduction is about one dollar per ton. On rolled iron or steel angles, channels, &c., weigh- ing less than 251 b. per lineal yard the reduction is 20 per cent. On rolled iron or steel beams, girders, joists, angles, channels, and structural shapes, weighing not less than 2.11 b., the reduction is from 16 dollars per ton to an average of 3 to 5 dollars. Wrought-iron tubing or pipes are reduced 120 per cent. On all contracts made before May 13 last, when the tariff resolutions were introduced, goods may enter Canada at the rate of duty in force prior to that date. All the above changes are in favour of , British manufactures. THE RUNCORN BANKRUPTCIES. At a special sitting of the Warrington Bankruptcy Court, yester- day, the bankruptcy. of William Farrell, an exten- sive builder at Runcorn, and a member of the Run- corn Improvement Commissioners, again came be- fore the Registrar (Mr. Nicholson.) Mr. Potter (who appeared on behalf pf the Official Receiyer) stated that a large claim had been made against a Mr. Kirby, but the Official Receiver had informed him (Mr. Potter) that arrangements had been made for Mr. Kirby to pay £350 or thereabouts in settlement of the claim. Under the circumstances it was con- sidered a useful settlement for both the creditors and the estate in general. The matter was very complicated, and if gone into would be an expen- sive litigation. He asked that the case might stand adjourned until the 15th July, and in the meantime the debtor would file an amended state of affairs, and it would leave time for the receiver and trus- tee to go into them.—The Registrar asked if the (payment of the sum mentioned would settle mat- ters between Mr. Kirby and the debtor.—Mr. Potter replied in the affirmative.—The Registrar said all seemed satisfactory, and the case was adjourned to the date mentionea.--The case of William James Shore was next mentioned by Mr. Potter, who said the account had not been thoroughly gone into by the Official Trustee, and he asked fof the case to be again adjourned. He formally questioned the debtor in reference to the latter 's conneetion with a Marine Insurance Co., the debtor stating that he was not an agent of the company, nor had he ac- cepted any premiums or risks on behalf of the company.:—The case was then adjourned until the 15th proximo. I THE INTENSE HEAT: SINGULAR RAILWAY BLOCK. —SO intense was the heat on Monday , afternoon that some of the rails on the. London and North- Western Railway between Ilityton and Prescot be- came twisted, and for a time put an entire stop to the whole of the traffic between Liverpool and the stations going north. The first train that was stopped was the 2-15 from Lime-street for Carlisle and Scotland, and before it could proceed on its journey it had to be got on to the up line, and be conveyed on it to the next station, involving a de- lay of about twenty minutes. Succeeding trains were similarly blocked. A gang of workmen were sent on from Lime-street Station by special train to repair the line immediately the stoppage was re- ported. The matter was put right by cutting off between three and four inches of each rail. The rails affected run along an exposed portion of the track known as the Bank. They are tight jointed for some distance, and this allows for no expansion. __

RUNCORN BOARD OF COMMISSIONERS. The annual meeting woe held at the Town Hell on Wed- needay morning. Mr. W. H. Linaker, the law clerk, took the chair pro. tem. Present—Messrs. P. Speskm n, S. Barker (surveyor.) APPOINTMENT OF CHAIRMAN. After an intim stion from the LaW Clerk that this was the first business, Mr. It. Shaw said that it was decided some time ago that the chairman should only bold office one year, and that view was now being carried out. At an in- formal meeting of the members on Monday evening it was resolved that Mr. Dobson eheuld be recommended to the Board that day, and he had great pleasure in moving that that gentleman should be appointed chairman for the ensu- ing 12 months. He was sure that Mr. Dobson would be able to fill the post with credit, and that the Board would be prepared to give him that assistance which would enable him to do so.—Mr. Imison said there seemed to be evident reluctance on the part of some gentleman to second the probably because be seconded the proposition at the informal meeting which was held. He now begged to second Mr. Shaw's motion, and be quite agreed with him that Mr. Dobson would undoubtedly carry out the tradi- tions of the chair, and that he would be a capable president. It Was the general opinion of the informal meeting that in Mr. Speakman they bad a very able chairman, and had it not been on account of a decision that had been arrived at, he had no doubt that many of the members would have bad much pleasure in asking him to retain the chairmanship for a longer period. Extracts from the public prints showed that the arrangement had been made, and they felt they could not go behind it. The reselu•ion was carried without dissent.—Mr. Hankinson asked if he could not move an amendment.—The Law Clerk: That was why I waited half a miaute before putting the motion.— Mr. Dobson then took the chair, and said he thanked the members for the honour they had conferred upon him. He hoped he should prove worthy of the confidence which they had reposed in him. He could not pretend to tread in the footprints of come of those gentlemen who had occupied that chair with such distinguished ability, and who had left their impress upon the business of the Board, which they as their successors were realising the henefit of. There were two characteristics which a chairman ought to possess. In the first place in conducting the business of the Board he ought to be strictly impartial; be should treat every member on an equality; and that he should endeavour to carry out. (Hear, hear.) Next, a chairman ought in some measure to understand the business of the Board. This was a delicate question, and they would excuse him from commenting upon it. Although he had been a member of the Board for 16 years, he felt still incompetent for the responsibilities of tbe office, but seeing that he was sur- rounded by such a number of clear-beaded business gentle- men, and feeling confident he should have their sympathy- and support, he under these circumstances accepted the responsibility. As they knew he had never sought the office, and he therefore valued it all the more that it had been freely offered to him. His only object had been to serve the ratepayers, and to add to the moral, social, and commercial prosperity of the town. He trusted that the life of every member would he spared, and that their health would be coot nued, and that this year would be a most happy and prosperous one. He entered upon this office knowing there was a clear and distinct understanding that the chairman, whoever he might be, had only to occupy it one year. If he were spired to the end of his year he should leave the chair to his successor with as much pleasure as he accepted it at the present time. (Hear, hear.) Ttlaftits TO MR. SPEARM &N. "DON'T YOU WORRY." TIOW SHREWD BUSINESS' MEN HAVE SOLVED
A GREAT PROBLEM.
"Is there a fatality among our prominent men ?" is a question that we often ask. It is a question that perplexes our leading medietl mar, and they are at a loss to know how to answer it.

We sometimes think that if the physicians would give part of the energy to the consideration of this question that they give to combatting other schools mf practice, it might be satisfactorily answered. The fights of " isms " reminds us often of the quarrels of some of our ancestors, who were only happy when they were annihilating each other. If Xllopathy makes a discovery that promises good to the race, Horeconrathv derides it and breaks down its influence. If ll.dnee,pathy m Aires a discovery that promises to be a boon to the race, Allopathy attacks it. It is absurd that these schools should fancy that all of good is in their methods and none in any other. Fortunately for the peopl4, the merit which these " isms " will not recognise, is recognised by the public, and this public recognition, taking the form of a demand upon the medical profession, eventually compels it to recognise

it. Is it possible that the question has been answered by shrewd business men? A prominent man once said to an inquirer. who asked him how he got rich, "I got rich be- cause I did things while other people were thinking about doing them." It seems to us that the yublic have recognised what this fatality is, and how it can be met, while the medical profession have been wrangling about ' it. By a.careful examination of insurance reports we find that there has been a sharp reform with reference to exami- nations (and that no man can now get any amount of insur- ance who has the least development of kidney disorder), because they find that sixty out of every hundred in this COuntry do. either directly or indirectly, staffer from kidney disease. Hence, no reliable company will incite a man ex- cept after a rigid urinary examination. This reminds us of a little instance which occurred a short time ago. A fellow-editor was an applicant for a respectable amount of insurance. Ha was rejected on ex- amination. because, unknown to himself, his kidneys were diseased. The shrewd agent, however, did not give up the case. He had an eye to business and to his commission, and Paid : "Don't you worry ; you get a half-dozen bottles Of Warner's SAFE Cure, take it according to directions, and in about a month come around, and we will have another examination. I know you will find yourself all right and will get your Policy." The editor exprei.sed surprise at the Agent's faith, but the latter replied: "This point is a valuable one. Very many insurance agents all over the country, when they find a customer rejected for this cause, give similar advice, and eventually he gets the insurance. What are we to infer from each circumstances? Have -shrewd insurance men, as well as other shrewd business men, found the secret answer to time inquiry? Is it possible that our columns have been proclaiming in the form of advertisements what has proved a blessing in disguise to millions, and yet by many ignored as an advertise- ment?

In our files we find thousands of strong testimonials for Warner's SAFE Cure, no two alike, which could not exist except upon a basis of truth • iudeed, they are pub- lished under a guarantee of £1,060 to any one who will disprove their correctness, and this off.ir has been standing for years. Hence we take the liberty of telling our friends that it is a duty that they owe to themselves to investigate the mat- ter and reflect carefully, for the statements published are subject to the refutation of the entire world. None have refuted them; on the c .nt,ary, hundreds of thousands have believed them and proved them true, and in believing have found the highest measure of satisfaction, that which money cannot buy, and money cannot take away.

WARIUNGTON AND THE QUEEN'S-

SPECIAL MEETING OF THE TOWN COUNCIL. On Tuesday evening a special meeting of the Town Council was held at the Town Hall to con- sider the question of celebrating the 50th anniver- sary of Her Majesty's accession to the throne, and to pass resolutions thereon. There were present the Mayor (Alderman Pickmere), Alderman Harri- son, Holmes ; Councillors Platt. W. Pierpoint, Greening, Barker, Brown, Jolley, IL Roberts, Tins- ley, Dixon, Bolton, Wright, Litton, Taylor, and Francomb.

div.head: LOYAL ADDRESS TO THE QUEEN.
div.p: LOYAL ADDRESS TO THE QUEEN.
The MAYOU said the first thing he would invite their attention to was a loyal address from the Mayor and Corporation to Her Majesty in connec- tion with the Jubilee.
The TOWN CLERK then read the address as fol- lows :

_ "To the Queen's most Excellent Majesty. May it please your Majesty.-- We, the Mayor, Aldermen, and Burgesses of the borough of War- \ rington, in the counties of Lancaster and Chester, desire to approach your Majesty on the auspicious occasion. ot your completing the 50th year of your reign, with respectful and sincere assurances of our loyalty to the and with earnest expressions a bur esteem and regard for your Majesty. The great interest your Majesty has taken in the wel- fare of all classes of your subjects evinced by your Majesty's visits to some of the large municipalities, I and by the deep sympathy expressed by your Majesty on any calamity falling upon them, evoke our warmest gratitude. We fervently congratulate I your Majesty upon the great reforms and improve- ments affected in our cities and towns during your Majesty's long and beneficient reign, and we I earnestly hope that your life may be blessed by con- , tinued family felicity, and that your Majesty may be low-,'' spared to reign over us." The MAYOR said the address was not too long,and was a very neatly written address in his opinion.' (Hear, hear.) He moved that the seal of the Cor- poration be affixed to the address, and that the same be forwarded to her Majesty. Alderman HoLmEs seconded this proposal, which was agreed to unanimously. _

div.head: SPECIAL SERVICE AT THE PARISH CHURCH.
div.p: SPECIAL SERVICE AT THE PARISH CHURCH.

The MAYOR said he had had a correspondence with the rector of Warrington with reference to the- Mayor and Corporation attending the Parish Church, the rector being, as they knew, the chap- lain of the Mayor and Corporation. In his letter to the'rector he suggested that some eminent preacher should, on an occasion like that, preach the sermon, and he snggested the Archdeacon of Warrington should be invited. The rector put himself into com- munication with the Archdeacon, but unfortunately he found that he had an appointment for the very day to preach elsewhere. On further correspond- enCe, however, the Arehdeacon got loose from his previous engagement, and then promised to come to Warrington to preach a sermon on the 26th inst. He (the Mayor) would, therefore, he at the Town Hall on the morning-of the 26th, and those members of the Corporation who wished might join him there, and they would go to the Parish Church. Alderman HARRISON said he hoped that the urgent ser- vices of a chaplain would not be rrqsirecl, or he was of raid they would be in an awkward position, because they had no chaplain. By some accident the chaplain was not re-ap- pointed, though he (Alderman Harrison) thought he ought to have been (Laughter.) The MAYOR: Ido not think that signifies very much. (Laughter.) A'derMan HARRISON: Well, I bone it does not.

The MAYOR s.tid he trusted the rector would do anything. for him in hi a religious capacity without being appointed chap'ain. Alderman HARRISON: I am sure he would. The matter then dropped. GRANT TO THE MAYOR.—THE ORANGEMEN AND THE

div.head: JUBILEE.
div.p: JUBILEE.

The MAYOR mentioned that he had made arrangements far the Corporation walking in tir °cession, and he had en- gaged the Volunteer Band to head them. He understood the Gas Committee had had under Consideration the matter of private illuminations in the town, and he was given to understand by the chairman of the Gas Committee that they hag agreed to allow gas for the illuminations at one- halt the price usually charged. He 3hould also ask them to allow a small sum for the illuminations in front of the Town Hall. The Jubilee Committee had arranged ta take the beautiful device that had been made at Dallam Forge 3113 fix it up in front of the Town Hall and he (the Mayor) wanted the Council to pay some little towards the fund for doing se. They were going to give, he thought, soreethini: like De for the device; and he had arranged for the Volun- teer Band to come for £7. He thought that about £3O would do, and he Aid not think that was too much for the Mayor of Warrington to ask the Corporation to allow him on an occasion Itke that. It they liked to make it .£5O he should be very glad, but he Should only ask them for £3O. The Tows CLEIRIC said that to be strictly in order the amount should he voted to the Mayor himself. Councillor DIXON moved that the sum of £5O ba allowed The Mayor for the purposes referred to. Alderman HoLmus seconded the proposal. Councillor PLATT hoped that nothing of a political char- acter would be allowed in connemion with the Jubilee cele- bration. Banners Which were likely to cause offence to any townsmen should not be allowed to be displayed. The MAYOR: If you want to do anything of that sort, Mr. Platt, I cannot allow it. (Hear, hear, and laughter.) Councillor H. ROBERTS said it was certainly reported that day, and it was no use blinking the fact, that the Orange body of Warrington as such had given notice ef their in- tention to take pert in the Jubilee celebrations. As they were not a frimdly society, not a benevolent society, and , certainly not a trade POCiO, y, but purely and simply a politi- cal institntion, he thought that certainly they should not be allowed to take part in the precession. At this point the Vote of £5O to the Mayor was carried Efl animousl y, after which
Alderman HARRISOII said be wished to say a word in res-

pact of Councillor Roberts' reference to the Orange Society • He was not an Orangeman himself, and never had been, but a circumstance had come under his notice some time ago which enabled him to say that the Orange Society was a friendly society because it contained within itself a sick club, mid when members were ill they were entitled to so much per week, and in the event of their death their sur- vivors were entitled to a certain sum. He thought that brought it within the category of a friendly society. But if it was the case that the Orange Society intended to take part in the procession with the view ef making some Poli- tical demonstration he was afraid it would mar the whole effect. He thought, however, that the interposition of the good offices of the Mayor with the Orange Society it they contemplated anything of the kind would be anfficient to deter them from it. (Hear, hear.) Councillor H. ROBERTS said he knew that there were numbers of people connected with the Jubilee who would take no part in it if the Orange body as such had a part in the procession. Councillor BOLTON thought that when they were voting £5O on behalf of the inhabitants of Warrington they ought to debar no one whether Orangemen, Roman Catholics or anything else. He objected to that class of thing being brought before the Council at all. Alderman Hanntsore did not see why the Orange Society should be excluded if they made no political demonstration. Councillor MARSH quite aoreed with Councillor Bolton and Alderman Harrison that they should not make diatinc- dons. If they did they would be making fish of one and flesh of another. He thought it should he left to the Mayor to stop any political demonstration if it were attempted to make one. (Hear, hear). The Mayoq sail it was a matter entirely for the Jubilee Committee. He did not see that the Corporation had any- thing to do with it. Councillor Dixow said that as a member of the Council he was not willing that the care of the town should be left to anybody but the Mayor. The MAYOR said he had not been aware that the Orange Society was going to walk. Councillor JOLLEY thought it wan purely a question as to whether the Orange body was a friendly society or not. If it was a friendly society they could as such take part in the procession, without making any political demonstration, and he did not see how the Jubilee Committee could say that they should not take part. The MAYOR: If it is a friendly society I should say de- cidedly that they have a right to take part in the proces- sion ; but that is what I don't know. , Councillor JOLLEY said if what Alderman Harrison sail was correct, he took it that the Orange Society was a , friendly society, and he had reason to believe that it was I correct.

Alderman BURGESS said if they were to determine in that Council Chamber what the Orange Society was, he would say that it was a friendly society, no doubt, bat it was a political society most certainly. Councillor BOLTON: They are all more or less. Alderman BURGESS, continuing, said the time had been when tbe Orange Society was placed under the ban. The MAYOR: Well, lam not up in these matters. (Laugh- ter.) The subject then dropped, and resolutions were passed to regulate vehicular traffic on the streets during the time of the Jubilee procession.

NO OX TO RE ROASTED.—THE IMPERIAL INSTITUTE. The MAYOR said he had a lett,r from a Mr. Taylor, of Liverpool,stating that he was a competent person to roast an ox, and offering his services. He would dress it, design the machinery for roasting it, cook it prcperly, Jic. (Laughter.) They, however, did not want an ox roasted at Warrington. The Mayor further announced that after the Jubilee festivi- ties wete over he should open an account at the three banks at Warringten on bAalf of the Imperial Institute. lie was not certain whether the Corporation wished to give anything or not, but he thought that as loyal men they ought to do something, and he for his part would do something for it, and he had no doubt other gentlemen in the town would do the lame. It had been suggested that they should join to- gether at a dinner on Tuesday evening, but as he had re- ceived Her Majesty's command to be present at the service which takes place on that day at Westminster Abbey, he should not be able to be present. Alderman HARRISON said if the Mayor were not present on such an occasion, it would be almost like the play of Hamlet with the part of Hamlet left out, and he suggested I that the dinner should be deferred till the Mayor could De present. (Hear, bear.) Alderman BURGESS: While regretting your absence very ' much, Mr. Mayor, your place would be so admirably filled ' by the Ex Mayor, that I hasdly see why the dinner shoald Ibe put off on that account (Laughter.) The subject then dropped. THE COUNCIL TO RE PHOTOGRAPHED.

The MAYOR Said he had received a letter from Alderman Webster, as to the members of the Council gettittg photo- graphed on an early day. Alderman Webster wrote to say that he would leave the matter in his hands. As Mr. Bowers had said that it would be better to have the photo- graph taken after the Jubilee was over,. ha would suggest that 12 o'clock on Thursday, the 30th, would be a very good time. This suggestion was agreed to. THE WALL IN FRONT OF THE TOWN HALL.

Alderman Heaufsulr said that almost all the towns in England were endeavouring to rival each other in com- mk.morating her Majesty's Jubilee. Some were building infirmaries, some were erecting libraries, some museums, and some one thing and some another, but most of them were putting up valuable and useful institutions. He had not I yet heard that Warrington was going to distinguish itself in that respect. It was very true that it possessed an ex- cellent museum and library, an excellent infirmary and art gallery, and he should like to move a resolution, which would show some means by which they could in a substan- tial manner do something without incurring a very large I expense to commemorate her Majrsty's Jubilee. 1 He proposed :—" That the wall at present standing at the front of the Town Hall be removed with all convenient speed, and a dwarf wall substituted, the same to be sur- mounted by a suitable palisading, with or without a pair of ; central gates, which latter question, together with all mat- ters of detail of and incidental to the carrying out of the said alteration, be left to the discretion of the Town Hall, Park, and Baths Committee and the General Purposes Corn-I mittee combined, and that the cost of doing the said werk be paid by the Corporation out of the public rates at a cost, if possible, not exceedina £350." (Hear, hew%) When he said £350 he felt sure that he bad left a wide margin, for they need not have an elaborate ornamentation, but a plain wall on the Erie 'of the present one and an unpretending palisade at the top of it, with suitable gates, and it would answer every purpose. Then would be revealed what was at present not seen by the inhabitants, namely, a Town Hail which was a structure of which no one need be ashamed. (Hear, heat.) Councillor .10t.LEg would second the resolution, though he would hardly go ea far as to spend £350. (Hear, hear.) , He thought the requirements of the case would be met if the I wall was taken down to about four feet, and the cost would , not amount to £5O; and when the proposed illumination I was put up it would enable thousands inWinmarleigh-street and Sankey-street to see it who would not otherwise be able , to do so. He contended that the wall could be reduced to I four feet in height in three days and would cost nothing because the atone would more than pay the cost. 1 Councillor WRIGHT strongly opposed the wall being dealt with in the piecemeal manner suggested by Councillor Jol- ley. If it was to be removed it ought to be done In an ar- tistic manner, and in a manner which would be a credit to the Corporation. (Hear, hear.) Alderman BurgekEsS wiabed to know if there was any proposition before the Council. A proposal had been made by Alderman Harrison, bat it had not been se- conded. The MAYOR : It has been seconded. Alderman BlittGEsS : Conditionally. Councillor MARSH thought that if the work was wofth doing at all it was worth doing well. The Corporation bad spent no money in connection with the Jubilee, and even if the cost of the removal of the wall was £3OO they could not complain. He, therefore, seconded Alderman's Harri- scn's;reaolution in its entirety. Alderman BURGESS : Are we not out of order in what we are doing? The agenda paper calls us together at half. past five "To consider the question of celebrating the 50th anniversary of her Majesty's accession to the throne, and to pass resolutions thereon." I consider that the proposi- tion made by Alderman Harrison does not come within the range of that business. I ask for the advice of the Town Clerk. The Tows CLERK: If it is done as a mode of celebrating the 50th anniversary-- Alderman HARRISON : Which it is. The Tows CLERK: Then I think it would come within the notice. But after the subject has been discussed 00 very often, and also dealt with as part of the arrangement to be carried out by the Jubilee Committee, it seems to me almost as though it was being rquerzed in. (Hear, hear.) Councillor BOLTON : Tne committee would not have it,

and we will not ha ,'e it. (Laughter.) Alderman BURGESS: I ask again if we can legitimately spend the amount of money foreshadowed by Alderman Harrison, the qa,stioe not having • been placed is such a manner on the agenda paper as to lead to the expectation that it would be discussed and disposed of to- night? The MAYOR: Really and truly it is a question for the Town Hall, Park, and Baths Committee. The better plan would have been for the resolution to have been carried by that Committee and then brought before the Council in the usual way. (Hear, hear.) Alderman BURGESS: Or let us have a notice on the paper and come here to discuss it. Alderman HOLMES said ke was glad the Mayor had deci- ded as he had done. Whenever that question of pulling down the wall rime up be should obj-ct to it. He had another proposition to make in place of that of Alderman Harrison, and it was that they should put up a handsome conservatory in the park, which would be an attraction to the people as well as instructive. Alderman HARRISON was willing to withdraw his propo- sition, and would have pleasure in seconding the suggestion which had been made by Councillor Jolley if he would bring it formally before the Council. only to remind you that little or no improvement has been made during the year. In conclasion, there is one too com- mon nuisance I feel it my dirty to bring before the commit- tea, not for the first time, bat I fear its importance bas I hardly been appreciated, and it is one of the very few per- manent sources of infectious disease left for the Health Committee to cope with and remedy. I refer to the de- fective condition of some of the sewers, and though it is a matter especially belonging to the Paving and , Sewerage Committee, and I have not the slightest wish to dictate to them, I think that energetic representations of the Health Committee may induce them to take more , active steps for the speedy remedy of the defect. It is an incontrovertible fact that vvnere the sewers are ill-constrac- ted, not sufficiently flushed, or imperfectly ventilated, there disease abounds. Zymotic disease, as a Nemesis, follows defective drainage. Indeed there are instances of outbreaks in which the origin of the disease can be attributed to nothir.g, but this source. The Borough Sur- veyor calls one sewer, that in Dial-street, 'an elongated cesspool." How can we expect the town to he in a sanitary state if such conditions are common ? I would respectfully Ibut earnestly urge the committee to take these matters into , immediate consideration.
The amendMent was then put, and Carried by a large majority.

Councillor JOLLEY endorsed what Councillor Platt had said. The committee bad remonstrated, and told the School Attendance officer to make representations to the school- masters, who endeavoured to override the committee. lie thought they ought to have some po yer to put a little pressure on thtse unreasonable schoolmasters and school- mistresses. To double the fees was a great shame, and the sooner it was remedied the better. (Rear, hear.) Alderman BURGESS said he should be glad ii one of the committee would be good enough to Wise them as to the reasons why masters of schools took the extraordinary
course to which reference had been made. There must be some strong reason.

Councillor BROWN said he had no heard a rational reason i assigned. but the conclusion the cemmiltee had arrived at ; was that what was done was very arbitrary indeed. The committee had done all they could with the schoolmasters, ; and he was very sorry to say they appeared to have made no impression. The only object they seemed to have—the gener.lity of them—was to exact the utmost penny out of ' the poor people's children who attended their schools.: They seemed to be totally destitute of anything like sym- pathetic feeling. It was immaterial to them whether a poor child went to school or not; their greatest desire was to pass a certain standard. The impression on the minds of the committee was that the schoolmasters and the teachers designedly put half•timers, when they came to their school, at a lower standard. Some schools in the town were far more generous than others, although some of them acted cruelly towards the poor children. Counctllor GREENING said that the question had been a &mime of great annoyance to the Committee. They had• I had on various occasions complaints made by very poor i people that double fees had been demanded from them. The j conclueiou at which the committee arrived was that the schoolmasters thought that by demanding double fees it I would make the children coins regularly and give up their ; work, which the poor people could not afford to allow them to do. (Hear, hear.) The schoolmasters could not get the children to pass as well as if they went all the time, and ' they consrquentiv lost some little portion of the grant. It was a matter of pounds, shillinge, and pence. Councillor FRANCOMB said he was one of the managers of of two or three large schools in the town, and he had never heard a single complaint from any manufacturer. He did not think it was right to blame the school teachers simply because they were not the responsible persons. They had not the Dower to deny admittance to any child—they dare not do so ; it was more than any schoolmaster in Warring- ton, or anywhere else, dared to do in the face of the school managers and in the face of the Education Department. He did not think it was so much a matter of pounds, shil- lings, and pence, bat with the schoolmaster and school- mistress any promotion they wished to get in the future depended on the percentage of passee; and as long as the Government expected a child to work half the day, and to go to school the other half, and pass the same rigid exami- nation, it was very unfair both to the schoolmaster and the , child. (Hear, hear.) The minutes were approved. Monks relative to the , question of a Free Lending Library, which was referred to • . the sub.committee appointed to meet the deputation. ; I It was explained that owing to the absence of Mr. R. .1 Davies the committee had not been ahle to consider the letter • I of Mr. Monks, after which the report was approved en the ;=t . , on or tne MAYOR, seconded by Alderman HARRISON.

CEMETERY COMMITTEE. The Registrar reported that the interments for the past four weeks were :—Adults, 43; minors, 74; stillborn and premature, 10; and for the corresponding period last year: —Adults, 36; minors, 37; stillborn and premature, 6. The receipts for the past four weeks were reported to be £BO 18i 11d, and for the corresponding period last year, £49 lOs 21.
Alderman HARRISON moved, and Councillor BROWN seconded, the confirmation of the minutes, and the motion was carried.
TOWN HALL, PARE, AND BATHS COMMITTEE.

It was reported that the i^come from the baths for the nest four weeks wag £lO 13s 4d, and for the corresponding period last year £24 15s 4d. It was resolved that the sum of £lO be voted to the hands for playing in the park during the summer ' • that the ground round the bond stand be asphalted, and that the tender of Mr. William Waring for the painting of the Town Hall buildings, &c., at £95 15s, be accepted.
The minutes of the committee were approved, on the motion of the MAYOR, snonded by Alderman liesaisoN.
OAS COMMITTEE.

An investigation had resulted in the discovery that there was a leakage of fifteen feet an hour. Councillor WRIGHT having seconded the motion, the minutes were approved.

This Committee recomm,mded that the firemen walk in the procession on the 20.12 June, and that the sum of £3 be voted to the men to defray the expences. Councillor ir RAN COMB moved and Councillor GREENING seconded, the confirmation of the minutes.

Councillor H. ROBERTS —For what purpose is the sum of £3 to be devoted to the firemen ? I cannot understand what expenses there will be. The MAYOR.—You don't know them as well as I do. (Izrughter.) The minutes were approved. _ LETTER FROM COUNCILLOR MACKIE.

At the conclusion of the meeting the MAYOR read part of letter received from Dr. Mackie, as follows :—" South- Dort, June 1211, 1887. De ir Mr. Mayor,—lt was kind and , in good taste of the Council to adjourn for a week to show 1 respect to the late Mr. George Crosfield. I have tried hard to be allowed to attend, but failed. Had I been present I could, however, only have said ditto ' to the many judicious remarks delivered by other members of the Council. I would seek to emphasize the appeals to our younger men to get ready for the work Warrington yet has for them. The week before I was stricken down I made an appeal to them in a lecture at Padgate, and ventured on giving some statistics of the consumption—so to speak—of public men since I knew Warrington. Since that lecture , it has been heavy—Wood, Rylands, Broadbent, Pearson, Crosfield, and several seriously ill. I think Mr. Crosfield merits in an especial way our praise for recognizing in so special a manner, and at a time when money was valuable 1 to him, the needs of Warrington for a Town Ball and a School of Art. He wisely became his own executor, and by ! judiciously giving early gave doubly." Io the part of the letter that the Mayor did not read the writer said :—" We ' need new men to come out, and, in the figures of scripture taken from Greek practices, to come out and be baptized for the dead. Ours is pre-eminently a mercantile town. Let our young men boar this in mind, and consecrate their youth, time, and money to make Warrington a great ' town." The Council then rose.

NOTES BY THE WAY.

A short time ago the Chancellor of the Exchequer when alluding to the private communications he received, re- marked upon the amazing anxiety of a large number of people for the imposition of new taxes and the getting rid of old ones. It seemed to be an invariable circumstance in connection with these private correspondents that the taxes tbey wished to get rid of were those which fell directly upon themselves, and the taxes which they wished to have imposed were those which would fall upon their neighbours. If the correspondent kept a dog he was almost sure to hold the conscientious opinion that an impost on cats would be good for the state, but if he, or rather she in this instance, happened to be possessed of a few feline pets, then the thing most to be commended was the raising of the price of the deg license to an almost prohibitive extent. It would seem that the members of the Wirral! Highway Board in their collective capacity, have a good deal of human nature about them, and, being no doubt mainly egriculturists, they find the highway rates hard to bear. They therefore look round to see if they can find anyone else to relieve them of their burdens, and who should they fix upon but the poor cyclist. They thereupon paces resolution in favour of putting a tax on bicycles and tricycles, and also determine to try to move their fellow waywardens in other districts to support their proposal. Fortunately there is very little about this pro- posed new agitation that need disturb the cyclist. It has always been observed that it is much easier to keep up the old taxes than to impose new ones, and Chancellors of Ex- chequer have an instinctive preference for the line of least resistance. And besides, no discriminating parry leader would in these days care about having the cyclist vote cast against him.

There was some heavy scoring on Saturday, in the match between Warrington and Liverpool. Liverpool occupied the whole of the afternoon with their innings, running up the sub- stantial score of 446 runs. The innings lasted four hours, giving 111 rune for each h•air. a s4mewhat remarkable per- formance. The highest individual score was 89 runs, ob- tained by Steel. At Manchester, on Saturday, Lancashire gained an easy victory over Derbyshire, mainly through the capital per- formances of Messrs. Eccles and Yates; the former, in his second innings, made 79 runs. Or. the Friday night Lan- cashire, with four of their best batstnen out in the last inn- ings, still wetted 89 runs to win. All chance of a close ter- mination, however' was speedily set aside on Saturday, for Messrs. Eccles and Yates, the not outs, added 92 runs in 55 minutes without losing another wicket. Mr. Eccles hit with brilliancy, his not-out innings including 11 fours, 3 threes, and a two. Both batsmen were deservedly cheered upon a fine performance. In the game between Westminster School and Lords and Commons, brought off at Westminster, on Saturday, the well-known Kentish cricketer, Lord Harris, played a fine, innings of 107, in which were 6 fours, 8 threes, and 17 twos, while several of the School batsmen hit with consi- derable freedom. In the end the name resulted in a draw, rather in favour of the Lords and Commons.

Surrey beat Oxford University, at Oxford, on Saturday by an innings and three runs, and Yorkshire came out 145 runs ahead azainst Leicesto.shire, at Dewsbury. ' Newton-le-Willows and Widnes met at Widnes en Satur- day and the play was of a fairly interesting character. For the vislto,s Longton and Glover made a long stand ; the former retiring for 52 and the latter 26. The total score was 114. The home team ran up a total of 41 for one wicket. At Lord's ground, the England Eleven on Wednesday gained a most decisive victory over the Marylebone Club by an innings and 117 rims. The M.C.C., at the drawing of stumps on Tuesday, wanted 281 runs to avert a single inning's defeat, with nine wickets ta fall, so their only chance was to stay in all day and make a draw of it. In this endeavour, however, they failed, and the match was finished off in a little less than two hours and a ball. Barnes played very fine cricket, and he and Flowers added 74 runs for the seventh wicket. Score :—M.C.C., 175 and 222; England, 514,

THE LATE MR. GEORGE CROSFIFLD. Sir,—The sad and sudden death of our kind and respec- ted townsman, the late Mr. George Crosfield, must have come as a great shock to many. "In the midst of life we are in death " is fully verified in the death of our respected friend. There is no doubt that his loss will be felt by a great many, for " His virtues were kind and rare." I think, sir, that this is now a fivourable opportunity to do something to keep in memory the kindly acts that as a town we have received from his hands. I would propose that a °citable monu- ment be set up in the park to show to our children that we have not been unmindful of our late townsman's generosity in putting us in possession of the beautiful park, which to many, both old and young, has become so very dear. I have no doubt, sir, that there are many who would like to give something towards such an object, and would do so willingly. My only reason for thus writing is that the subject may by these few lines be brought to the notice of the public. If anything can be done I shall be glad to give a subscription towards it. Trusting someone will enter upon the question who bas greater ability than I possess, I enclose card and remain respectfully yours, E. B.

JOHN BRIGHT ON OPPRESSION. Sir,—ln presence of the agonising scenes at Bodyke, it would be very appropriate if you would print what Mr. Bright said forty-three years ago, of our " oppressors " in general. It was at Covent Garden Theatre, on February 27, 1844; he spoke thus There is one thing which, above all, the people should get rid of, namely, their reverence for even the worthless portion of the aristocracy. It is a false and worthless idolatry; a bowing down to Baal. I rever- ence and respect the laws when they are the embodiment of just principles; but I cannot countenance the reverence paid by the people to those who oppress, grind them down, and scourge them. I hope the day will arrive when they will throw off the butdens with which they are oppressed by the aristocracy, and stand forth the bravest, the freest, and the most virtuous people on the face of the earth." Not a word is necessary to apply this impressive utterance, andevery one of your readers will realise the significance of it as applic- able to the momentous deeds now enacting in Ireland. I live in the fervent hope of seeing our once "dread com- mander, in shape and gesture proudly eminent," once more on the side of the "oppressed ; " so let us wait respectfully, I until the "excess of glory obscured" has passed sway, and his " ori&nal brightness" return with new-furbished arms himself to scourge the oppressor.

THE HOWLEY INTERCEPTING • DEPOT. Sir.—l don't like to complain without a cause, and I would be the last man to do it. In the above case I, as a pro- perty owner, have lodged a complaint with the authorities of the town, but I doubt not that it will be like all similar complaints—it will receive "our careful consideration," and then lodged in the "pigeon hole." By your permission, Mr. Editor, I would like to make my complaintmore widely known, because I am speaking on behalf of the inhabitants of this neighbourhood, who are continually complaining of a sickening Smell arising from the working of this nurtur- ing nest of disease. lam now alluding to the manure in- tercepting depot at Howley. At certain times the stench is over-bearing and sickening, creating even a dislike for the food which one is about to eat, and vomiting ensuing. What it will be when the hot days come on and continue one hardly dare contemplate. Manufacturers are harassed and fined for turning out of their chimneys a little hlack smoke; tenants are ordered to Dull down any am ill shed they may have erected in their yards, lest they might ac- cumulate anything offensive, and yet these abominable, expensive, experimental nuisances are brought to the work- ing-man's very deer. Before this change, the vans contain- ing the tube were, as they were filled, at once driven off to Longford, but under the new arrangement one part of this neighbourhood is invested by a three-fold service of passing vans which create a nuisance ten times greater than before. Why should a low-land population like this be mule to endure a nuisance which would not be tolerated a single day in some of the brighter spots in the town? Although men may hold high position in a town, they have no right to try expeliments like these (which I believe I am not too old to see prove a failure) at the expense of the health otone Dart of the population. There are even higher tribunals than any town posseesee where matters of this serieus kind can be submitted, and I own that that step should be a laet extremity; but I seriously warn the authorities of the ex- isting nuisance, and I exnect by them it will be seriously entertained, because if through these stink dens an epi- demic of some serious character should break out, a remedy might come too late.—Yonrs resnectfullv. WILLIAM DIOGLE.

div.head: SUNDAY SCHOOL TEACHERS AND THE JUBILEE.
div.p: SUNDAY SCHOOL TEACHERS AND THE JUBILEE.

Sir,—lf we may judge from the opinions we hear fre- quently expressed, some people are seeking to throw a good deal of discredit on Sunday school managers and teachers in connection with the Jubilee. These people point to the unexpectedly large number of scholars returned as attending the Sunday schools, and then forthwith come to the conclu- sion that the teachers of all or pert of the schools have magnified their attendances in order to get hold of a larger capitation grant than is properly their due. Now, sir, it seems to me that the conclusion of these people is both I hasty and uncharitable. Everybody who has the least ac- quaintance with Sunday schools knows that a large section of the scholars is very migratory in its habits. A scholar belonging to this class attends, perhaps, a Church of Eng- land school fora few Sundays, then a Wetdeyan, and very likely the school of some other delomination soon afterwards. The name of such a scholar as this is, therefore, very likely OA two or three or more registers, and would no doubt be returned two or three or mere times to the Jubilee Cammit- tee for the sixpence per head. But, as far as the teachers in each instance know he is a bona fide scholar, though rather irregular in his attendance, and may be expected to turn up when there is a treat in the wind. In ctses of this kind, no one can fairly say that teachers are trying to get more than their proper share of the Jubilee fund. Yet it seems to me that this is the only ground for the reflections that are made against the Sunday school teachers. It is a fact, of course, that the scholar referred to can only be with one school on the day of the tr.,at, and that consequently the other schools which returned him will get a sixpence they are not enti- tled to. But with regard to this, I think if their critics would not be so hasty in their judgments they will find they have entertained an entirely unjeet opinion of the integrity of Sunday school teachers. Th.se teachers are, as a spsaker at the Jubilee meeting last week said, the teachers of morality in the town. They know that the money awarded from the Jubilee fund to their Sunday schools ha e been givsn on the understanding that for every sixpence given a scholar would be provided for. What is more, they know, as "teachers of morality," that while morality at its strictest would not condemn for inadvertent- ly returning more scholars than may turn up on the Jubilee day, it would at its loosest condemn their conduct as utterly unjustifiable if they retained money w`.ich was awarded them on the understanding that these scholars would turn up. I think, therefore, if those who are saying uncharitable things about the conductors of Sunday schools would just wait a week or two, they will be put to the blush by the unhesitating manner in which these same conductors will restitute what they find has bees given them from the Ju- bilee fund in excess of the number of the scholars who attend their treat. I have not the least doubt that the money that will in this way be returned to the jubilee fund will , assist very materially in providing some Permanent com- memoration of the jubilee in Warrington.—Yours. !cc., A PAST SCHOLAR.

JUBILEE WEF—K— IN WARRINGTON. Sir,—l sincerely hope, as a working-man, that you will favour me once more with a little corner in your valuable columns with a few brief observations regarding "Cohn Clout's" reply to my letter in your issue of the 4•11 inst. I was very much disappointed. as well as surprised, that I did sot receive more support from the hand of the work- ing-men in town on their own behalf for the Jubilee week than my letter merited. This is a time that the working- man's voice has as much right to be heard as the voice of the employer of labour, when it is within the bounds of sense and reason; and now,..Mr. Editor, as your columns are open for the advocation of causes for the poor as well as the rich, we hope that eventually my suggestion will not fall to the ground, irrespective of any opposition directly or in- directly, but have the consideration and speedy approval of those gentlemen who may be kindly dimosed to confer such a boon on the working-men of this town, by allowing them at least the 20th and 21st day's wages if they don't work. I would also suggest that those who work on either of these two days should be Old two days' wages for each day, or, if not, at least time and a half. , Regarding paying all employes the fall week's wages, whether closed a part or the whole of Jubilee week, it is left entirely to the generosity of snch masters of labour as can see their way to do so ; and, as stated in my former letter, they would not be the losers by it in the long run. We have various examples of wages paid to clerks and employes' in several establishments throughout the Kingdom and I America as a Jubilee bonus, and therefore, I ask, why not in Warrington? Were it not for the working-man, with his hard-earned low wages in our time, where would the employers of labour be; and how could they have their sixpenny cigars, six months at the seaside, with their carriages and pair with flunkies, and their champagne ad libitum? These are not the bare necessaries of life, which the working-man ha? a struggle to eet in a very bare way, but luxuries indulged in in some cases to a greater extent than necessary. Though trade is in some departments of industry gradu- ally and slowly improving, we know it has been a bard time for all; but masters had their day, and took advantage of it, and now it is instant dismissal for a workine-man in many canes for a very small fault, as the master knows full well he has a multitude of servants always ready in the field to step in for such low wages as can hardly co,mand the hare neesssaries of life, never sneaking about the ordin- ary luxuries that a man is in need of after his week's toil- ing along. I am exceedingly sorry, sir, if I take up too much of your valuable space, but this is a suggestion for the employers of labour in Warrington to kindly consider, and is an event which I earnestly hope the working-men in town will look back upon in years to come with jmv and rejoicing. We are aware of the kind and courteous manner the subecrip,ion list has been raised to defray the Jubilee sxpenses, hat I think my suggestion, notwithstanding that, should meet with the desired pport, and rank with the other good works that are being done. Warrington, 15th June, 1887.

A special correspohdent on board the Norhates Castle, telegraphing from Leith on Thursday morning, says :—lt has been a splendid run to Leith. The weather has been fine and calm, but rather hazy. We passed the Sleuth Hound off Lowestoft. She was then leading, followed by the tw) big schooners, the Selene and the Owendoline. We have seen nothing of the other eight yachts which started from Southend on Tuesday afternoon.
